sourceDesc.p: The text of this edition is the Perseus Project's double-keyboarded transcription (c. 2003) of The Complete Works of William Shakespeare, ed. William George Clark and William Aldis Wright (Garden City, New York: Nelson Doubleday, Inc.), 2 vols. (OCLC 08687211; Tufts University's Tisch Library holds two catalog records for this set, both giving the date only as "19--"). Love's Labor's Lost is in volume 1, consulted in the Internet Archive copy bwb_KT-315-451_1 (pp. 56-83); its date of printing is not confirmed. That edition reprints the Globe text in a setting of its own, with American spellings, which the transcription keeps. In some readings the transcription departs from both the copy-text and the Globe; the cause has not been established.

The Globe line numbering is not taken from the copy-text. It is read from two page-image witnesses to the Globe itself, printed from the same plates two decades apart: The Works of William Shakespeare, Cambridge and London: Macmillan, 1866 (HathiTrust miun.aba6868.0001.001, University of Michigan copy, catalog record 000241315) and The Works of William Shakespeare, London: Macmillan, 1887 (Internet Archive worksofwilliamsh0000shak_y3h8, Trent University copy, OCLC 1158473505).

editorialDecl.p: Words and structure -- divisions, speakers, speeches, stage directions, and verse lines where the copy-text sets verse -- are the double-keyboarded text, unaltered. Where a witness page disagrees with it over a word, the transcription stands and the disagreement is recorded in the project's reports.

The Globe lineation was regenerated from the witnesses in 2026. Each printed row of the witness page was classified by its typography, Globe lines were assembled from those rows, and the resulting count was checked on every page against every line number printed in that page's margins; a page whose count disagreed with any printed number was not accepted. In eleven places in this play the page's typography does not show where a Globe line begins: two speeches that may share a verse line, a speech's line continued on a row set flush with the margin, or a row set as though it completed the line above which the Globe numbers as a line of its own. These were decided individually, from the page images and the printed line numbers and, where the page is silent, from the line division of the Folger edition, Love's Labor's Lost, ed. Barbara A. Mowat and Paul Werstine, Folger Digital Texts, version 0.5 (Washington, DC: Folger Shakespeare Library, 2015), as distributed in the Shakespeare Drama Corpus (ShakeDraCor, play shake000007; github.com/dracor-org/shakedracor, commit c34c2d4). The Folger was consulted only for its division of shared lines, never for words or numbers. Each decision is recorded in the project's data tables.

The Globe line numbers previously carried by the Perseus edition were transcribed from the copy-text and are not retained. They are consistent with the numbering below, but were placed by a different convention.
First Folio through-line numbers are not carried by this edition. They remain in the Perseus P4 edition.

encodingDesc.p: <milestone unit="line" ed="Globe"> marks the first word of a Globe line, and every Globe line carries one, numbered. A Globe line may occupy more than one printed row: a verse line too long for the column, or a line shared between two speakers. <lb/> marks each printed row that begins no Globe line. A Globe milestone therefore also marks the start of a printed row, and reconstructing the page's rows requires reading both elements.

The @part attribute, which marks the parts of a verse line shared between speakers, is retained from the Perseus P4 edition and was not regenerated. It does not always agree with the Globe's division of shared lines; where the two differ, the Globe milestones govern the numbering.

div.head: SCENE I
div.stage:
Enter FERDINAND, king of NAVARRE, BIRON,
LONGAVILLE, and DUMAIN.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l:
Let fame, that all hunt after in their
lives,
Live register'd upon our brazen tombs
And then grace us in the disgrace of death;
When, spite of cormorant devouring Time,
The endeavour of this present breath may buy

That honour which shall bate his scythe's keen
edge
And make us heirs of all eternity.
Therefore, brave conquerors,--for so you are,
That war against your own affections
And the huge army of the world's desires,--
Our late edict shall strongly stand in force:
Navarre shall be the wonder of the world;
Our court shall be a little Academe,
Still and contemplative in living art.
You three, Biron, Dumain, and Longaville,
Have sworn for three years' term to live with me
My fellow-scholars and to keep those statutes
That are recorded in this schedule here:

Your oaths are pass'd; and now subscribe your
names,
That his own hand may strike his honour down
That violates the smallest branch herein:
If you are arm'd to do as sworn to do,
Subscribe to your deep oaths, and keep it too.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l:
I am resolved; 'tis but a three years'
fast:
The mind shall banquet, though the body pine:
Fat paunches have lean pates, and dainty bits
Make rich the ribs, but bankrupt quite the wits.

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.l: My loving lord, Dumain is mortified:
The grosser manner of these world's delights
He throws upon the gross world's baser slaves:
To love, to wealth, to pomp, I pine and die;
With all these living in philosophy.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l: I can but say their protestation over;
So much, dear liege, I have already sworn,
That is, to live and study here three years.
But there are other strict observances;
As, not to see a woman in that term,
Which I hope well is not enrolled there;
And one day in a week to touch no food
And but one meal on every day beside,
The which I hope is not enrolled there;
And then, to sleep but three hours in the night,
And not be seen to wink of all the day--
When I was wont to think no harm all night
And make a dark night too of half the day--
Which I hope well is not enrolled there:
O, these are barren tasks, too hard to keep,
Not to see ladies, study, fast, not sleep!

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l:
Your oath is pass'd to pass away from
these.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l:
Let me say no, my liege, an if you
please:
I only swore to study with your grace
And stay here in your court for three years' space.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l:
You swore to that, Biron, and to
the rest.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l:
By yea and nay, sir, then I swore
in jest.
What is the end of study? let me know.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l:
Why, that to know, which else we
should not know.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l:
Things hid and barr'd, you mean,
from common sense?

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Ay, that is study's god-like recompense.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l: Come on, then; I will swear to study so,
To know the thing I am forbid to know:
As thus,--to study where I well may dine,
When I to feast expressly am forbid;
Or study where to meet some mistress fine,
When mistresses from common sense are hid;
Or, having sworn too hard a keeping oath,
Study to break it and not break my troth.
If study's gain be thus and this be so,
Study knows that which yet it doth not know:
Swear me to this, and I will ne'er say no.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l:
These be the stops that hinder study
quite
And train our intellects to vain delight.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l:
Why, all delights are vain; but that
most vain,
Which with pain purchased doth inherit pain:
As, painfully to pore upon a book

To seek the light of truth; while truth the
while
Doth falsely blind the eyesight of his look:
Light seeking light doth light of light beguile:
So, ere you find where light in darkness lies,
Your light grows dark by losing of your eyes.
Study me how to please the eye indeed
By fixing it upon a fairer eye,
Who dazzling so, that eye shall be his heed
And give him light that it was blinded by.
Study is like the heaven's glorious sun
That will not be deep-search'd with saucy looks:
Small have continual plodders ever won
Save base authority from others' books.
These earthly godfathers of heaven's lights
That give a name to every fixed star
Have no more profit of their shining nights

Than those that walk and wot not what
they are.
Too much to know is to know nought but fame;
And every godfather can give a name.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l:
How well he's read, to reason against
reading!

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.l:
Proceeded well, to stop all good
proceeding!

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l:
He weeds the corn and still lets grow
the weeding.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l:
The spring is near when green geese
are a-breeding.

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.l: How follows that?

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l: Fit in his place and time.

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.l: In reason nothing.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l: Something then in rhyme.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Biron is like an envious sneaping frost,

That bites the first-born infants of
the spring.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l: Well, say I am; why should proud summer boast
Before the birds have any cause to sing?
Why should I joy in any abortive birth?
At Christmas I no more desire a rose
Than wish a snow in May's new-fangled mirth;
But like of each thing that in season grows.
So you, to study now it is too late,
Climb o'er the house to unlock the little gate.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l:
Well, sit you out: go home, Biron:
adieu.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l:
No, my good lord; I have sworn to
stay with you:
And though I have for barbarism spoke more
Than for that angel knowledge you can say,
Yet confident I'll keep what I have swore
And bide the penance of each three years' day.
Give me the paper; let me read the same;
And to the strict'st decrees I'll write my name.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l:
How well this yielding rescues thee
from shame!

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.p: 'Item, That no woman shall come within a mile of my court:' Hath this been proclaimed?

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.p: Four days ago.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.p: Let's see the penalty. Reads'On pain of losing her tongue.' Who devised this penalty?

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.p: Marry, that did I.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.p: Sweet lord, and why?

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.p:
To fright them hence with that dread
penalty.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.p: A dangerous law against gentility! Reads'Item, If any man be seen to talk with a woman within the term of three years, he shall endure such public shame as the rest of the court can possibly devise.'
sp.l: This article, my liege, yourself must break;
For well you know here comes in embassy

The French king's daughter with yourself to
speak--
A maid of grace and complete majesty--
About surrender up of Aquitaine
To her decrepit, sick and bedrid father:
Therefore this article is made in vain,
Or vainly comes the admired princess hither.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l:
What say you, lords? why, this was
quite forgot.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l: So study evermore is overshot:
While it doth study to have what it would
It doth forget to do the thing it should,
And when it hath the thing it hunteth most,
'Tis won as towns with fire, so won, so lost.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l:
We must of force dispense with this
decree;
She must lie here on mere necessity.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l: Necessity will make us forsworn

Three thousand times within this three years'
space;
For every man with his affects is born,
Not by might mastered but by special grace:
If I break faith, this word shall speak for me;
I am forsworn on 'mere necessity.'

So to the laws at large I write my name:
Subscribes.
And he that breaks them in the least degree
Stands in attainder of eternal shame:
Suggestions are to other as to me;
But I believe, although I seem so loath,
I am the last that will last keep his oath.
But is there no quick recreation granted?

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l:
Ay, that there is. Our court, you know,
is haunted
With a refined traveller of Spain;
A man in all the world's new fashion planted,
That hath a mint of phrases in his brain;
One whom the music of his own vain tongue
Doth ravish like enchanting harmony;
A man of complements, whom right and wrong
Have chose as umpire of their mutiny:
This child of fancy, that Armado hight,
For interim to our studies shall relate
In high-born words the worth of many a knight
From tawny Spain lost in the world's debate.
How you delight, my lords, I know not, I;
But, I protest, I love to hear him lie
And I will use him for my minstrelsy.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l: Armado is a most illustrious wight,
A man of fire-new words, fashion's own knight.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l:
Costard the swain and he shall be our
sport;

And so to study, three years is but short.
Enter DULL with a letter, and COSTARD.

sp.speaker: Dull.
sp.p: Which is the duke's own person?

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.p: This, fellow: what wouldst?

sp.speaker: Dull.
sp.p: I myself reprehend his own person, for I am his grace's tharborough; but I would see his own person in flesh and blood.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.p: This is he.

sp.speaker: Dull.
sp.p: Signior Arme--Arme--commends you. There's villany abroad: this letter will tell you more.

sp.speaker: Cost.
sp.p: Sir, the contempts thereof are as touching me.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: A letter from the magnificent Armado.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.p: How low soever the matter, I hope in God for high words.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.p: A high hope for a low heaven: God grant us patience!

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.p: To hear? or forbear laughing?

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.p: To hear meekly, sir, and to laugh moderately; or to forbear both.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.p: Well, sir, be it as the style shall give us cause to climb in the merriness.

sp.speaker: Cost.
sp.p: The matter is to me, sir, as concerning Jaquenetta. The manner of it is, I was taken with the manner.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.p: In what manner?

sp.speaker: Cost.
sp.p: In manner and form following, sir; all those three: I was seen with her in the manor-house, sitting with her upon the form, and taken following her into the park; which, put together, is in manner and form following. Now, sir, for the manner,--it is the manner of a man to speak to a woman: for the form,-- in some form.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.p: For the following, sir?

sp.speaker: Cost.
sp.p: As it shall follow in my correction: and God defend the right!

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: Will you hear this letter with attention?

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.p: As we would hear an oracle.

sp.speaker: Cost.
sp.p: Such is the simplicity of man to hearken after the flesh.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: 'Great deputy, the welkin's vicegerent and sole dominator of Navarre, my soul's earth's god, and body's fostering patron.'

sp.speaker: Cost.
sp.p: Not a word of Costard yet.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: 'So it is,'--

sp.speaker: Cost.
sp.p: It may be so: but if he say it is so, he is, in telling true, but so.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: Peace!

sp.speaker: Cost.
sp.p: Be to me and every man that dares not fight!

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: No words!

sp.speaker: Cost.
sp.p: Of other men's secrets, I beseech you.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: 'So it is, besieged with sable-coloured melancholy, I did commend the black-oppressing humour to the most wholesome physic of thy health-giving air; and, as I am a gentleman, betook myself to walk. The time when. About the sixth hour; when beasts most graze, birds best peck, and men sit down to that nourishment which is called supper: so much for the time when. Now for the ground which; which, I mean, I walked upon: it is ycleped thy park. Then for the place where; where, I mean, I did encounter that obscene and preposterous event, that draweth from my snow-white pen the ebon-colored ink, which here thou viewest, beholdest, surveyest, or seest; but to the place where; it standeth north-north-east and by east from the west corner of thy curious-knotted garden: there did I see that low-spirited swain, that base minnow of thy mirth,'--

sp.speaker: Cost.
sp.p: Me?

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: 'that unlettered small-know- ing soul,'--

sp.speaker: Cost.
sp.p: Me?

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: 'that shallow vassal,'--

sp.speaker: Cost.
sp.p: Still me?

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: 'which, as I remember, hight Costard,--

sp.speaker: Cost.
sp.p: O, me!

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: 'sorted and consorted, contrary to thy established proclaimed edict and continent canon, which with,--O, with--but with this I passion to say wherewith,--

sp.speaker: Cost.
sp.p: With a wench.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: 'with a child of our grandmother Eve, a female; or, for thy more sweet understanding, a woman. Him I, as my ever-esteemed duty pricks me on, have sent to thee, to receive the meed of punishment, by thy sweet grace's officer, Anthony Dull; a man of good repute, carriage, bearing, and estimation.'

sp.speaker: Dull.
sp.p: Me, an't shall please you; I am Anthony Dull.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p:
'For Jaquenetta,--so is the weaker vessel called which I apprehended with the aforesaid swain,--I keep her as a vessel of the law's fury; and shall, at the least of thy sweet notice, bring her to trial. Thine, in all compliments of devoted and heart-burning heat of duty.
DON ADRIANO DE ARMADO.'

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.p: This is not so well as I looked for, but the best that ever I heard.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: Ay, the best for the worst. But, sirrah, what say you to this?

sp.speaker: Cost.
sp.p: Sir, I confess the wench.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: Did you hear the proclamation?

sp.speaker: Cost.
sp.p: I do confess much of the hearing it but little of the marking of it.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: It was proclaimed a year's imprisonment, to be taken with a wench.

sp.speaker: Cost.
sp.p: I was taken with none, sir: I was taken with a damsel.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: Well, it was proclaimed 'damsel.'

sp.speaker: Cost.
sp.p: This was no damsel, neither, sir; she was a virgin.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: It is so varied, too; for it was proclaimed 'virgin.'

sp.speaker: Cost.
sp.p: If it were, I deny her virginity: I was taken with a maid.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: This maid will not serve your turn, sir.

sp.speaker: Cost.
sp.p: This maid will serve my turn, sir.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: Sir, I will pronounce your sentence: you shall fast a week with bran and water.

sp.speaker: Cost.
sp.p: I had rather pray a month with mutton and porridge.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: And Don Armado shall be your keeper.
My lord Biron, see him deliver'd o'er:
And go we, lords, to put in practice that
Which each to other hath so strongly sworn.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l: I'll lay my head to any good man's hat,
These oaths and laws will prove an idle scorn.
Sirrah, come on.

sp.speaker: Cost.
sp.p: I suffer for the truth, sir; for true it is,I was taken with Jaquenetta, and Jaquenetta is a true girl; and therefore welcome the sour cup of prosperity! Affliction may one day smile again; and till then, sit thee down, sorrow! Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.p: Boy, what sign is it when a man of great spirit grows melancholy?

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: A great sign, sir, that he will look sad.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.p: Why, sadness is one and the self-same thing, dear imp.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: No, no; O Lord, sir, no.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.p: How canst thou part sadness and melancholy, my tender juvenal?

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: By a familiar demonstration of the working, my tough senior.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.p: Why tough senior? why tough senior?

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: Why tender juvenal? why tender juvenal?

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.p: I spoke it, tender juvenal, as a congruent epitheton appertaining to thy young days, which we may nominate tender.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: And I, tough senior, as an appertinent title to your old time, which we may name tough.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.l: Pretty and apt.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: How mean you, sir? I pretty, and my saying apt? or I apt, and my saying pretty?

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.p: Thou pretty, because little.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: Little pretty, because little. Wherefore apt?

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.p: And therefore apt, because quick.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: Speak you this in my praise, master?

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.l: In thy condign praise.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: I will praise an eel with the same praise.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.p: What, that an eel is ingenious?

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: That an eel is quick.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.p: I do say thou art quick in answers: thou heatest my blood.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: I am answered, sir.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.p: I love not to be crossed.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: He speaks the mere contrary; crosses love not him.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.p: I have promised to study three years with the duke.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: You may do it in an hour, sir.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.p: Impossible.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: How many is one thrice told?

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.p: I am ill at reckoning; it fitteth the spirit of a tapster.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: You are a gentleman and a gamester, sir.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.p: I confess both: they are both the varnish of a complete man.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: Then, I am sure, you know how much the gross sum of deuce-ace amounts to.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.p: It doth amount to one more than two.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: Which the base vulgar do call three.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.p: True.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: Why, sir, is this such a piece of study? Now here is three studied, ere ye'll thrice wink: and how easy it is to put' years' to the word 'three,' and study three years in two words, the dancing horse will tell you.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.p: A most fine figure!

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: To prove you a cipher.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.p: I will hereupon confess I am in love: and as it is base for a soldier to love, so am I in love with a base wench. If drawing my sword against the humour of affection would deliver me from the reprobate thought of it, I would take Desire prisoner, and ransom him to any French courtier for a new-devised courtesy. I think scorn to sigh: methinks I should outswear Cupid. Comfort, me, boy: what great men have been in love?

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: Hercules, master.

sp.speaker: Arm.
Moth.
sp.p: Samson, master: he was a man of good carriage, great carriage, for he carried the town-gates on his back like a porter: and he was in love.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.p: O well-knit Samson! strong-jointed Samson! I do excel thee in my rapier as much as thou didst me in carrying gates. I am in love, too. Who was Samson's love, my dear Moth?

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: A woman, master.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.p: Of what complexion?

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: Of all the four, or the three, or the two, or one of the four.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.p: Tell me precisely of what complexion.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: Of the sea-water green, sir.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.p: Is that one of the four complexions?

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: As I have read, sir; and the best of them too.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.p: Green indeed is the colour of lovers; but to have a love of that colour, methinks Samson had small reason for it. He surely affected her for her wit.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: It was so, sir; for she had a green wit.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.p: My love is most immaculate white and red.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: Most maculate thoughts, master, are masked under such colours.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.p: Define, define, well-educated infant.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: My father's wit and my mother's tongue, assist me!

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.p: Sweet invocation of a child; most pretty and pathetical!

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.l: If she be made of white and red,
Her faults will ne'er be known,
For blushing cheeks by faults are bred
And fears by pale white shown:
Then if she fear, or be to blame,
By this you shall not know,
For still her cheeks possess the same
Which native she doth owe.
sp.p: A dangerous rhyme, master, against the reason of white and red.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.p: Is there not a ballad, boy, of the King and the Beggar?

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: The world was very guilty of such a ballad some three ages since: but I think now 'tis not to be found; or, if it were, it would neither serve for the writing nor the tune.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.p: I will have that subject newly writ o'er, that I may example my digression by some mighty precedent. Boy, I do love that country girl that I took in the park with the rational hind Costard: she deserves well.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: To be whipped; and yet a better love than my master.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.p: Sing, boy; my spirit grows heavy in love.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: And that's great marvel, loving a light wench.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.p: I say, sing.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p:
Forbear till this company be past.
Enter DULL, COSTARD, and JAQUENETTA.

sp.speaker: Dull.
sp.p: Sir, the duke's pleasure is, that you keep Costard safe: and you must suffer him to take no delight nor no penance; but a' must fast three days a week. For this damsel, I must keep her at the park: she is allowed for the day-woman. Fare you well.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.p: I do betray myself with blushing. Maid!

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.p: Man?

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.p: I will visit thee at the lodge.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.p: That's hereby.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.p: I know where it is situate.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.p: Lord, how wise you are!

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.p: I will tell thee wonders.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.p: With that face?

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.p: I love thee.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.p: So I heard you say.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.p: And so, farewell.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.p: Fair weather after you!

sp.speaker: Dull.
sp.p:
Come, Jaquenetta, away!
Exeunt Dull and Jaquenetta.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.p: Villain, thou shalt fast for thy offences ere thou be pardoned.

sp.speaker: Cost.
sp.p: Well, sir, I hope, when I do it, I shall do it on a full stomach.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.p: Thou shalt be heavily punished.

sp.speaker: Cost.
sp.p: I am more bound to you than your fellows, for they are but lightly rewarded.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.p: Take away this villain; shut him up.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: Come, you transgressing slave; away!

sp.speaker: Cost.
sp.p: Let me not be pent up, sir: I will fast, being loose.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: No, sir; that were fast and loose: thou shalt to prison.

sp.speaker: Cost.
sp.p: Well, if ever I do see the merry days of desolation that I have seen, some shall see.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: What shall some see?

sp.speaker: Cost.
sp.p:
Nay, nothing, Master Moth, but what they look upon. It is not for prisoners to be too silent in their words; and therefore I will say nothing: I thank God I have as little patience as another man; and therefore I can be quiet.
Exeunt Moth and Costard.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.p: I do affect the very ground, which is base, where her shoe, which is baser, guided by her foot, which is basest, doth tread. I shall be forsworn, which is a great argument of falsehood, if I love. And how can that be true love which is falsely attempted? Love is a familiar; Love is a devil: there is no evil angel but Love. Yet was Samson so tempted, and he had an excellent strength; yet was Solomon so seduced, and he had a very good wit. Cupid's butt-shaft is too hard for Hercules' club; and therefore too much odds for a Spaniard's rapier. The first and second cause will not serve my turn; the passado he respects not, the duello he regards not: his disgrace is to be called boy; but his glory is to subdue men. Adieu, valour! rust, rapier! be still, drum! for your manager is in love; yea, he loveth. Assist me, some extemporal god of rhyme, for I am sure I shall turn sonnet. Devise, wit; write, pen; for I am for whole volumes in folio. Exit.

div.head: SCENE I
div.stage:
Enter the Princess of France, ROSALINE, MARIA,
KATHARINE, BOYET, Lords, and other
Attendants.

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.l:
Now, madam, summon up your
dearest spirits:
Consider who the king your father sends,
To whom he sends, and what's his embassy:
Yourself, held precious in the world's esteem,
To parley with the sole inheritor
Of all perfections that a man may owe,
Matchless Navarre; the plea of no less weight
Than Aquitaine, a dowry for a queen.
Be now as prodigal of all dear grace
As Nature was in making graces dear
When she did starve the general world beside
And prodigally gave them all to you.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l:
Good Lord Boyet, my beauty, though
but mean,
Needs not the painted flourish of your praise:
Beauty is bought by judgement of the eye,
Not utter'd by base sale of chapmen's tongues:
I am less proud to hear you tell my worth
Than you much willing to be counted wise
In spending your wit in the praise of mine.
But now to task the tasker: good Boyet,
You are not ignorant, all-telling fame
Doth noise abroad, Navarre hath made a vow,
Till painful study shall outwear three years,
No woman may approach his silent court:
Therefore to's seemeth it a needful course,
Before we enter his forbidden gates,
To know his pleasure; and in that behalf,
Bold of your worthiness, we single you
As our best-moving fair solicitor.
Tell him, the daughter of the King of France,
On serious business, craving quick dispatch,
Importunes personal conference with his grace:
Haste, signify so much; while we attend,
Like humble-visaged suitors, his high will.

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.l: Proud of employment, willingly I go.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l:
All pride is willing pride, and yours
is so. Exit Boyet.
Who are the votaries, my loving lords,
That are vow-fellows with this virtuous duke?

sp.speaker: First Lord.
sp.l: Lord Longaville is one.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l: Know you the man?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l:
I know him, madam: at a
marriagefeast,
Between Lord Perigort and the beauteous heir
Of Jaques Falconbridge, solemnized
In Normandy, saw I this Longaville:
A man of sovereign parts he is esteem'd;
Well fitted in arts, glorious in arms:
Nothing becomes him ill that he would well.
The only soil of his fair virtue's gloss,
If virtue's gloss will stain with any soil,
Is a sharp wit match'd with too blunt a will;

Whose edge hath power to cut, whose will still
wills
It should none spare that come within his power.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l:
Some merry mocking lord, belike; is
't so?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l:
They say so most that most his
humours know.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l:
Such short-lived wits do wither as
they grow.
Who are the rest?

sp.speaker: Kath.
sp.l:
The young Dumain; a
well-accomplished youth,
Of all that virtue love for virtue loved:
Most power to do most harm, least knowing ill;
For he hath wit to make an ill shape good,
And shape to win grace though he had no wit.
I saw him at the Duke Alencon's once;
And much too little of that good I saw
Is my report to his great worthiness.

sp.speaker: Ros.
sp.l: Another of these students at that time
Was there with him, if I have heard a truth.
Biron they call him; but a merrier man,
Within the limit of becoming mirth,
I never spent an hour's talk withal:
His eye begets occasion for his wit;
For every object that the one doth catch
The other turns to a mirth-moving jest,
Which his fair tongue, conceit's expositor,
Delivers in such apt and gracious words
That aged ears play truant at his tales
And younger hearings are quite ravished;
So sweet and voluble is his discourse.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l:
God bless my ladies! are they all in
love,
That every one her own hath garnished
With such bedecking ornaments of praise?

sp.speaker: First Lord.
sp.l:
Here comes Boyet.
Re-enter BOYET.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l: Now, what admittance, lord?

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.l:
Navarre had notice of your fair
approach;
And he and his competitors in oath
Were all address'd to meet you, gentle lady,
Before I came. Marry, thus much I have learnt:
He rather means to lodge you in the field,
Like one that comes here to besiege his court,
Than seek a dispensation for his oath,
To let you enter his unpeopled house.

Here comes Navarre.
Enter KING, LONGAVILLE, DUMAIN, BIRON,
and Attendants.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l:
Fair princess, welcome to the court of
Navarre.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.p: 'Fair' I give you back again; and 'welcome' I have not yet: the roof of this court is too high to be yours; and welcome to the wide fields too base to be mine.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l:
You shall be welcome, madam, to my
court.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l:
I will be welcome, then: conduct me
thither.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l:
Hear me, dear lady; I have sworn an
oath.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l:
Our Lady help my lord! he'll be
forsworn.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l:
Not for the world, fair madam, by my
will.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l:
Why, will shall break it; will and
nothing else.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Your ladyship is ignorant what it is.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l:
Were my lord so, his ignorance were
wise,
Where now his knowledge must prove ignorance.
I hear your grace hath sworn out house-keeping:
'Tis deadly sin to keep that oath, my lord,
And sin to break it.
But pardon me, I am too sudden-bold:
To teach a teacher ill beseemeth me.
Vouchsafe to read the purpose of my coming,
And suddenly resolve me in my suit.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Madam, I will, if suddenly I may.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l: You will the sooner, that I were away;
For you'll prove perjured if you make me stay.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l:
Did not I dance with you in Brabant
once?

sp.speaker: Ros.
sp.l:
Did not I dance with you in Brabant
once?

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.p: I know you did.

sp.speaker: Ros.
sp.l:
How needless was it then to ask the
question!

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l: You must not be so quick.

sp.speaker: Ros.
sp.l:
'Tis 'long of you that spur me with such
questions.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l:
Your wit's too hot, it speeds too fast,
'twill tire.

sp.speaker: Ros.
sp.l: Not till it leave the rider in the mire.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.p: What time o' day?

sp.speaker: Ros.
sp.p: The hour that fools should ask.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.p: Now fair befall your mask!

sp.speaker: Ros.
sp.p: Fair fall the face it covers!

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.p: And send you many lovers!

sp.speaker: Ros.
sp.p: Amen, so you be none.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.p: Nay, then will I be gone.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Madam, your father here doth intimate
The payment of a hundred thousand crowns;
Being but the one half of an entire sum
Disbursed by my father in his wars.
But say that he or we, as neither have,
Received that sum, yet there remains unpaid

A hundred thousand more; in surety of the
which,
One part of Aquitaine is bound to us,
Although not valued to the money's worth.
If then the king your father will restore
But that one half which is unsatisfied,
We will give up our right in Aquitaine,
And hold fair friendship with his majesty.
But that, it seems, he little purposeth,
For here he doth demand to have repaid
A hundred thousand crowns; and not demands,
On payment of a hundred thousand crowns,
To have his title live in Aquitaine;
Which we much rather had depart withal
And have the money by our father lent
Than Aquitaine so gelded as it is.
Dear princess, were not his requests so far
From reason's yielding, your fair self should make
A yielding 'gainst some reason in my breast
And go well satisfied to France again.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l:
You do the king my father too much
wrong
And wrong the reputation of your name,
In so unseeming to confess receipt
Of that which hath so faithfully been paid.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: I do protest I never heard of it;
And if you prove it, I'll repay it back
Or yield up Aquitaine.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l: We arrest your word.
Boyet, you can produce acquittances
For such a sum from special officers
Of Charles his father.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Satisfy me so.

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.l:
So please your grace, the packet is not
come
Where that and other specialties are bound:
To-morrow you shall have a sight of them.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: It shall suffice me: at which interview
All liberal reason I will yield unto.
Meantime receive such welcome at my hand
As honour without breach of honour may
Make tender of to thy true worthiness:
You may not come, fair princess, in my gates;
But here without you shall be so received
As you shall deem yourself lodged in my heart,
Though so denied fair harbour in my house.
Your own good thoughts excuse me, and farewell:
To-morrow shall we visit you again.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l:
Sweet health and fair desires consort
your grace!

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l:
Thy own wish wish I thee in every
place! Exit.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l:
Lady, I will commend you to mine
own heart.

sp.speaker: Ros.
sp.p: Pray you, do my commendations; I would be glad to see it.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.p: I would you heard it groan.

sp.speaker: Ros.
sp.p: Is the fool sick?

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.p: Sick at the heart.

sp.speaker: Ros.
sp.p: Alack, let it blood.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.p: Would that do it good?

sp.speaker: Ros.
sp.p: My physic says 'ay.'

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.p: Will you prick't with your eye?

sp.speaker: Ros.
sp.l: No point, with my knife.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l: Now, God save thy life!

sp.speaker: Ros.
sp.l: And yours from long living!

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l: I cannot stay thanksgiving. Retiring.

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.l:
Sir, I pray you, a word: what lady is
that same?

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.l:
The heir of Alencon, Katharine her
name.

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.l:
A gallant lady. Monsieur, fare you
well. Exit.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l:
I beseech you a word: what is she in
the white?

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.l:
A woman sometimes, an you saw her
in the light.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l:
Perchance light in the light. I desire
her name.

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.l:
She hath but one for herself; to desire
that were a shame.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.p: Pray you, sir, whose daughter?

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.p: Her mother's, I have heard.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.p: God's blessing on your beard!

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.p: Good sir, be not offended. She is an heir of Falconbridge.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.p: Nay, my choler is ended. She is a most sweet lady.

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.p:
Not unlike, sir, that may be.
Exit Long.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.p: What's her name in the cap?

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.p: Rosaline, by good hap.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.p: Is she wedded or no?

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.p: To her will, sir, or so.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.p: You are welcome, sir: adieu.

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.l:
Farewell to me, sir, and welcome to
you. Exit Biron.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l:
That last is Biron, the merry madcap
lord:
Not a word with him but a jest.

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.l: And every jest but a word.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l:
It was well done of you to take him at
his word.

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.l:
I was as willing to grapple as he was
to board.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Two hot sheeps, marry.

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.l: And wherefore not ships?

No sheep, sweet lamb, unless we feed on your
lips.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l:
You sheep, and I pasture: shall that
finish the jest?

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.l:
So you grant pasture for me.
Offering to kiss her.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Not so, gentle beast:
My lips are no common, though several they be.

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.l: Belonging to whom?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: To my fortunes and me.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l:
Good wits will be jangling; but,
gentles, agree:
This civil war of wits were much better used

On Navarre and his book-men; for here 'tis
abused.

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.l:
If my observation, which very seldom
lies,
By the heart's still rhetoric disclosed with eyes,
Deceive me not now, Navarre is infected.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.p: With what?

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.l:
With that which we lovers entitle
affected.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.p: Your reason?

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.l:
Why, all his behaviours did make their
retire
To the court of his eye, peeping through desire:

His heart, like an agate, with your print
impress'd,
Proud with his form, in his eye pride express'd:
His tongue, all impatient to speak and not see,
Did stumble with haste in his eyesight to be;
All senses to that sense did make their repair,
To feel only looking on fairest of fair:
Methought all his senses were lock'd in his eye,
As jewels in crystal for some prince to buy;

Who, tendering their own worth from where they
were glass'd,
Did point you to buy them, along as you pass'd:
His face's own margent did quote such amazes
That all eyes saw his eyes enchanted with gazes.
I'll give you Aquitaine and all that is his,
An you give him for my sake but one loving kiss.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l: Come to our pavilion: Boyet is disposed.

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.l:
But to speak that in words which his
eye hath disclosed.
I only have made a mouth of his eye,
By adding a tongue which I know will not lie.

sp.speaker: Ros.
sp.l:
Thou art an old love-monger and speakest
skilfully.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l:
He is Cupid's grandfather and learns
news of him.

sp.speaker: Ros.
sp.l:
Then was Venus like her mother, for her
father is but grim.

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.l: Do you hear, my mad wenches?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: No.

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.l: What then, do you see?

sp.speaker: Ros.
sp.l: Ay, our way to be gone.

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.l: You are too hard for me. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.p: Warble, child; make passionate my sense of hearing.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: Concolinel. Singing.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.p: Sweet air! Go, tenderness of years; take this key, give enlargement to the swain, bring him festinately hither: I must employ him in a letter to my love.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.l: Master, will you win your love with a French brawl?

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.l: How meanest thou? brawling in French?

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: No, my complete master: but to jig off a tune at the tongue's end, canary to it with your feet. humor it with turning up your eyelids, sigh a note and sing a note, sometime through the throat, as if you swallowed love with singing love, sometime through the nose, as if you snuffed up love by smelling love; with your hat penthouse-like o'er the shop of your eyes; with your arms crossed on your thin-belly doublet like a rabbit on a spit; or your hands in your pocket like a man after the old painting; and keep not too long in one tune, but a snip and away. These are complements, these are humours; these betray nice wenches, that would be betrayed without these; and make them men of note--do you note me?--that most are affected to these.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.l: How hast thou purchased this experience?

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: By my penny of observation.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.p: But O,--but O,--

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.l: 'The hobby-horse is forgot.'

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.l: Callest thou my love 'hobby-horse'?

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: No, master; the hobby-horse is but a colt, and your love perhaps a hackney. But have you forgot your love?

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.p: Almost I had.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: Negligent student! learn her by heart.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.l: By heart and in heart, boy.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: And out of heart, master: all those three I will prove.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.l: What wilt thou prove?

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: A man, if I live; and this, by, in, and without, upon the instant: by heart you love her, because your heart cannot come by her; in heart you love her, because your heart is in love with her; and out of heart you love her, being out of heart that you cannot enjoy her.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.p: I am all these three.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: And three times as much more, and yet nothing at all.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.l: Fetch hither the swain: he must carry me a letter.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: A message well sympathized; a horse to be ambassador for an ass.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.p: Ha, ha! what sayest thou?

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: Marry, sir, you must send the ass upon the horse, for he is very slow-gaited. But I go.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.p: The way is but short: away!

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: As swift as lead, sir.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.p: The meaning, pretty ingenious? Is not lead a metal heavy, dull, and slow?

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.l:
Minime, honest master; or rather,
master, no.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.l: I say lead is slow.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.l: You are too swift, sir, to say so:
Is that lead slow which is fired from a gun?

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.l: Sweet smoke of rhetoric!
He reputes me a cannon; and the bullet, that's he:
I shoot thee at the swain.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.l: Thump then and I flee. Exit.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.l:
A most acute juvenal; volable and free
of grace!

By thy favour, sweet welkin, I must sigh in thy
face:
Most rude melancholy, valour gives thee place.

My herald is return'd.
Re-enter MOTH with COSTARD.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.l:
A wonder, master! here's a costard
broken in a shin.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.l:
Some enigma, some riddle: come, thy
l'envoy; begin.

sp.speaker: Cost.
Arm.
sp.p: By virtue, thou enforcest laughter; thy silly thought my spleen; the heaving of my lungs provokes me to ridiculous smiling. O, pardon me, my stars! Doth the inconsiderate take salve for l'envoy, and the word l'envoy for a salve?

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p:
Do the wise think them other? is not
l'envoy a salve?

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.l:
No, page: it is an epilogue or discourse,
to make plain

Some obscure precedence that hath tofore been
sain.
I will example it:
The fox, the ape and the humble-bee,
Were still at odds, being but three.
There's the moral. Now the l'envoy.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.l: I will add the l'envoy. Say the moral again.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.l: The fox, the ape, the humble-bee,
Were still at odds, being but three.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.l: Until the goose came out of door,
And stay'd the odds by adding four.
sp.p: Now will I begin your moral, and do you follow with my l'envoy.
sp.l: The fox, the ape and the humble-bee,
Were still at odds, being but three.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.l: Until the goose came out of door,
Staying the odds by adding four.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.l: A good l'envoy, ending in the goose: would you desire more?

sp.speaker: Cost.
sp.l:
The boy hath sold him a bargain, a goose,
that's flat.
Sir, your pennyworth is good, an your goose be fat.

To sell a bargain well is as cunning as fast and
loose:
Let me see; a fat l'envoy; ay, that's a fat goose.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.l:
Come hither, come hither. How did
this argument begin?

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.l:
By saying that a costard was broken
in a shin.
Then call'd you for the l'envoy.

sp.speaker: Cost.
sp.l:
True, and I for a plantain: thus came
your argument in;

Then the boy's fat l'envoy, the goose that you
bought;
And he ended the market.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.p: But tell me; how was there a costard broken in a shin?

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: I will tell you sensibly.

sp.speaker: Cost.
sp.p: Thou hast no feeling of it, Moth: I will speak that l'envoy:
sp.l: I Costard, running out, that was safely within,
Fell over the threshold, and broke my shin.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.l: We will talk no more of this matter.

sp.speaker: Cost.
sp.l: Till there be more matter in the shin.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.l: Sirrah Costard, I will enfranchise thee.

sp.speaker: Cost.
sp.p: O, marry me to one Frances: I smell some l'envoy, some goose, in this.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.p: By my sweet soul, I mean setting thee at liberty, enfreedoming thy person: thou wert immured, restrained, captivated, bound.

sp.speaker: Cost.
sp.p: True, true; and now you will be my purgation and let me loose.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.p: I give thee thy liberty, set thee from durance; and, in lieu thereof, impose on thee nothing but this: bear this significant[giving a letter] to the country maid Jaquenetta: there is remuneration; for the best ward of mine honor is rewarding my dependents. Moth, follow. Exit.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.l:
Like the sequel, I. Signior Costard,
adieu.

sp.speaker: Cost.
sp.l:
My sweet ounce of man's flesh! my
incony Jew! Exit Moth. Now will I look to his remuneration. Remuneration! O, that's the Latin word for three farthings: three farthings--remuneration.-- 'What's the price of this inkle?'--'One penny.'--'No, I'll give you a remuneration:' why, it carries it. Remuneration! why, it is a fairer name than French crown. I will never buy and sell out of this word.
Enter BIRON.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.p: O, my good knave Costard! exceedingly well met.

sp.speaker: Cost.
sp.p: Pray you, sir, how much carnation ribbon may a man buy for a remuneration?

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.p: What is a remuneration?

sp.speaker: Cost.
sp.p: Marry, sir, halfpenny farthing.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l: Why, then, three-farthing worth of silk.

sp.speaker: Cost.
sp.l: I thank your worship: God be wi' you!

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l: Stay, slave; I must employ thee:
As thou wilt win my favour, good my knave,
Do one thing for me that I shall entreat.

sp.speaker: Cost.
sp.p: When would you have it done, sir?

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.p: This afternoon.

sp.speaker: Cost.
sp.p: Well, I will do it, sir: fare you well.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.p: Thou knowest not what it is.

sp.speaker: Cost.
sp.l: I shall know, sir, when I have done it.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l: Why, villain, thou must know first.

sp.speaker: Cost.
sp.l: I will come to your worship to-morrow morning.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.p: It must be done this afternoon.
Hark, slave, it is but this:
sp.l: The princess comes to hunt here in the park,
And in her train there is a gentle lady;

When tongues speak sweetly, then they name her
name,
And Rosaline they call her: ask for her;
And to her white hand see thou do commend

This seal'd-up counsel. There's thy guerdon; go.
Giving him a shilling.

sp.speaker: Cost.
sp.p: Gardon, O sweet gardon! better than remuneration, a 'leven-pence farthing better: most sweet gardon! I will do it, sir, in print. Gardon! Remuneration! Exit.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l: And I, forsooth, in love! I, that
have been love's whip;
A very beadle to a humorous sigh;
A critic, nay, a night-watch constable;
A domineering pedant o'er the boy;
Than whom no mortal so magnificent!
This wimpled, whining, purblind, wayward boy;
This senior-junior, giant-dwarf, Dan Cupid;
Regent of love-rhymes, lord of folded arms,
The anointed sovereign of sighs and groans,
Liege of all loiterers and malcontents,
Dread prince of plackets, king of codpieces,
Sole imperator and great general
Of trotting 'paritors:--O my little heart:--
And I to be a corporal of his field,
And wear his colours like a tumbler's hoop!
What, I! I love! I sue! I seek a wife!
A woman, that is like a German clock,
Still a-repairing, ever out of frame,
And never going aright. being a watch,
But being watch'd that it may still go right!
Nay, to be perjured, which is worst of all;
And, among three, to love the worst of all;
A wightly wanton with a velvet brow,
With two pitch-balls stuck in her face for eyes;
Ay, and, by heaven, one that will do the deed
Though Argus were her eunuch and her guard:
And I to sigh for her! to watch for her!
To pray for her! Go to; it is a plague
That Cupid will impose for my neglect
Of his almighty dreadful little might.

Well, I will love, write, sigh, pray, sue and
groan:
Some men must love my lady and some Joan. [Exit.

div.head: SCENE I
div.stage:
Enter the Princess, and her train, a Forester,
BOYET, ROSALINE, MARIA, and KATHARINE.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l:
Was that the king, that spurr'd his
horse so hard
Against the steep uprising of the hill?

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.l: I know not; but I think it was not he.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l:
Whoe'er a' was, a' show'd a mounting
mind.
Well, lords, to-day we shall have our dispatch:
On Saturday we will return to France.
Then, forester, my friend, where is the bush
That we must stand and play the murderer in?

sp.speaker: For.
sp.l:
Hereby, upon the edge of yonder
coppice;
A stand where you may make the fairest shoot.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l: I thank my beauty, I am fair that shoot,
And thereupon thou speak'st the fairest shoot.

sp.speaker: For.
sp.l: Pardon me, madam, for I meant not so.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l:
What, what? first praise me and again
say no?
O short-lived pride! Not fair? alack for woe!

sp.speaker: For.
sp.l: Yes, madam, fair.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l: Nay, never paint me now:
Where fair is not, praise cannot mend the brow.
Here, good my glass, take this for telling true:
Fair payment for foul words is more than due.

sp.speaker: For.
sp.l:
Nothing but fair is that which you
inherit.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l:
See, see, my beauty will be saved by
merit!
O heresy in fair, fit for these days!
A giving hand, though foul, shall have fair praise.
But come, the bow: now mercy goes to kill,
And shooting well is then accounted ill.
Thus will I save my credit in the shoot:
Not wounding, pity would not let me do't:
If wounding, then it was to show my skill,
That more for praise than purpose meant to kill.
And out of question so it is sometimes,
Glory grows guilty of detested crimes,

When, for fame's sake, for praise, an outward
part,
We bend to that the working of the heart;
As I for praise alone now seek to spill

The poor deer's blood, that my heart means no
ill.

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.l:
Do not curst wives hold that
selfsovereignty
Only for praise sake, when they strive to be
Lords o'er their lords?

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l:
Only for praise: and praise we may
afford
To any lady that subdues a lord.

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.l:
Here comes a member of the
commonwealth.
Enter COSTARD.

sp.speaker: Cost.
sp.p: God dig-you-den all! Pray you, which is the head lady?

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.p: Thou shalt know her, fellow, by the rest that have no heads.

sp.speaker: Cost.
sp.p: Which is the greatest lady, the highest?

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.p: The thickest and the tallest.

sp.speaker: Cost.
sp.l:
The thickest and the tallest! it is so;
truth is truth.

An your waist, mistress, were as slender as my
wit,

One o' these maids' girdles for your waist should
be fit.

Are not you the chief woman? you are the
thickest here.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l:
What's your will, sir? what's your
will?

sp.speaker: Cost.
sp.l:
I have a letter from Monsieur Biron to
one Lady Rosaline.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l:
O, thy letter, thy letter! he's a good
friend of mine:
Stand aside, good bearer. Boyet, you can carve;
Break up this capon.

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.l: I am bound to serve.
This letter is mistook, it importeth none here;
It is writ to Jaquenetta.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l: We will read it, I swear.

Break the neck of the wax, and every one give
ear.

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.p: 'By heaven, that thou art fair, is most infallible; true, that thou art beauteous; truth itself, that thou art lovely. More fairer than fair, beautiful than beauteous, truer than truth itself, have commiseration on thy heroical vassal! The magnanimous and most illustrate king Cophetua set eye upon the pernicious and indubitate beggar Zenelophon; and he it was that might rightly say, Veni, vidi, vici; which to annothanize in the vulgar, --O base and obscure vulgar!--videlicet, He came, saw, and overcame: he came, one; saw two; overcame, three. Who came? the king: why did he come? to see: why did he see? to overcome: to whom come he? to the beggar: what saw he? the baggar: who overcame he? the beggar. The conclusion is victory: on whose side? the king's. The captive is enriched: on whose side? the beggar's. The catastrophe is a nuptial: on whose side? the king's: no, on both in one, or one in both. I am the king; for so stands the comparison: thou the beggar; for so witnesseth thy lowliness. Shall I command thy love? I may: shall I enforce thy love? I could: shall I entreat thy love? I will. What shalt thou exchange for rags? robes; for tittles? titles; for thyself? me. Thus, expecting thy reply, I profane my lips on thy foot, my eyes on thy picture, and my heart on thy every part. Thine, in the dearest design of industry, DON ADRIANO DE ARMADO.'
sp.l: Thus dost thou hear the Nemean lion roar

'Gainst thee, thou lamb, that standest as his
prey.
Submissive fall his princely feet before,
And he from forage will incline to play:
But if thou strive, poor soul, what art thou then?
Food for his rage, repasture for his den.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l:
What plume of feathers is he that
indited this letter?

What vane? what weathercock? did you ever
hear better?

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.l:
I am much deceived but I remember
the style.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l:
Else your memory is bad, going o'er
it erewhile.

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.l:
This Armado is a Spaniard, that keeps
here in court;

A phantasime, a Monarcho, and one that makes
sport
To the prince and his bookmates.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l: Thou fellow, a word:
Who gave thee this letter?

sp.speaker: Cost.
sp.l: I told you; my lord.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l: To whom shouldst thou give it?

sp.speaker: Cost.
sp.l: From my lord to my lady.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l: From which lord to which lady?

sp.speaker: Cost.
sp.l:
From my lord Biron, a good master of
mine,
To a lady of France that he call'd Rosaline.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l:
Thou hast mistaken his letter. Come,
lords, away. [To Ros.[

Here, sweet, put up this; 'twill be
thine another day.
[Exeunt Princess and train.

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.l: Who is the suitor? who is the suitor?

sp.speaker: Ros.
sp.l: Shall I teach you to know?

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.l: Ay, my continent of beauty.

sp.speaker: Ros.
sp.l: Why, she that bears the bow.
Finely put off!

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.l:
My lady goes to kill horns; but, if
thou marry,

Hang me by the neck, if horns that year
miscarry.
Finely put on!

sp.speaker: Ros.
sp.l: Well, then, I am the shooter.

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.l: And who is your deer?

sp.speaker: Ros.
sp.l:
If we choose by the horns, yourself
come not near.
Finely put on, indeed!

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l:
You still wrangle with her, Boyet, and
she strikes at the brow.

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.l:
But she herself is hit lower: have I
hit her now?

sp.speaker: Ros.
sp.p: Shall I come upon thee with an old saying, that was a man when King Pepin of France was a little boy, as touching the hit it?

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.p: So I may answer thee with one as old, that was a woman when Queen Guinover of Britain was a little wench, as touching the hit it.

sp.speaker: Ros.
sp.l: Thou canst not hit it, hit it, hit it,
Thou canst not hit it, my good man.

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.l: An I cannot, cannot, cannot,
An I cannot, another can.

sp.speaker: Cost.
sp.l:
By my troth, most pleasant: how both
did fit it!

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l:
A mark marvellous well shot, for they
both did hit it.

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.l:
A mark! O, mark but that mark! A
mark, says my lady!

Let the mark have a prick in't, to mete at, if it
may be.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l:
Wide o' the bow hand! i' faith, your
hand is out.

sp.speaker: Cost.
sp.l:
Indeed, a' must shoot nearer, or he'll
ne'er hit the clout.

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.l:
An if my hand be out, then belike
your hand is in.

sp.speaker: Cost.
sp.l:
Then will she get the upshoot by
cleaving the pin.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l:
Come, come, you talk greasily; your
lips grow foul.

sp.speaker: Cost.
sp.l:
She's too hard for you at pricks, sir:
challenge her to bowl.

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.l:
I fear too much rubbing. Good night,
my good owl. Exeunt Boyet and Maria.

sp.speaker: Cost.
sp.l:
By my soul, a swain! a most simple
clown!

Lord, Lord, how the ladies and I have put him
down!

O' my troth, most sweet jests! most incony
vulgar wit!

When it comes so smoothly off, so obscenely, as
it were, so fit.
Armado o' th' one side,--O, a most dainty man!
To see him walk before a lady and to bear her fan!

To see him kiss his hand! and how most sweetly
a' will swear!
And his page o' t' other side, that handful of wit!
Ah, heavens, it is a most pathetical nit!

Sola, sola! [Shout within.
[Exit Costard, running.

div.head: SCENE II
div.stage: Enter HOLOFERNES, SIR NATHANIEL, and DULL.

sp.speaker: Nath.
sp.p: Very reverend sport, truly; and done in the testimony of a good conscience.

sp.speaker: Hol.
sp.p: The deer was, as you know, sanguis, in blood; ripe as the pomewater, who now hangeth like a jewel in the ear of caelo, the sky, the welkin, the heaven; and anon falleth like a crab on the face of terra, the soil, the land, the earth.

sp.speaker: Nath.
sp.p: Truly, Master Holofernes, the epithets are sweetly varied, like a scholar at the least: but, sir, I assure ye, it was a buck of the first head.

sp.speaker: Hol.
sp.p: Sir Nathaniel, haud credo.

sp.speaker: Dull.
sp.l: 'Twas not a haud credo; 'twas a pricket.

sp.speaker: Hol.
sp.p: Most barbarous intimation! yet a kind of insinuation, as it were, in via, in way, of explication; facere, as it were, replication, or rather, ostentare, to show, as it were, his inclination, after his undressed, unpolished, uneducated, unpruned, untrained, or rather, unlettered, or ratherest, unconfirmed fashion, to insert again my haud credo for a deer.

sp.speaker: Dull.
sp.l: I said the deer was not a haud credo; 'twas a pricket.

sp.speaker: Hol.
sp.l: Twice-sod simplicity, bis coctus!

O thou monster Ignorance, how deformed dost
thou look!

sp.speaker: Nath.
sp.p:
Sir, he hath never fed of the dainties
that are bred in a book; he hath not eat paper, as it were; he hath not drunk ink: his intellect is not replenished; he is only an animal, only sensible in the duller parts: And such barren plants are set before us, that we
thankful should be, Which we of taste and feeling are, for those parts
that do fructify in us more than he. For as it would ill become me to be vain,
indiscreet, or a fool, So were there a patch set on learning, to see
him in a school: But omne bene, say I; being of an old father's
mind, Many can brook the weather that love not the wind.

sp.speaker: Dull.
sp.l:
You two are book-men: can you tell me
by your wit

What was a month old at Cain's birth, that's not
five weeks old as yet?

sp.speaker: Hol.
sp.l:
Dictynna, goodman Dull; Dictynna,
goodman Dull.

sp.speaker: Dull.
sp.l: What is Dictynna?

sp.speaker: Nath.
sp.l: A title to Phoebe, to Luna, to the moon.

sp.speaker: Hol.
sp.l:
The moon was a month old when Adam
was no more.

And raught not to five weeks when he came to
five-score.
The allusion holds in the exchange.

sp.speaker: Dull.
sp.l:
'Tis true indeed: the collusion holds in
the exchange.

sp.speaker: Hol.
sp.l: God comfort thy capacity! I say, the
allusion holds in the exchange.

sp.speaker: Dull.
sp.p: And I say, the pollusion holds in the exchange; for the moon is never but a month old: and I say beside that, 'twas a pricket that the princess killed.

sp.speaker: Hol.
sp.p: Sir Nathaniel, will you hear an extemporal epitaph on the death of the deer? And, to humor the ignorant, call I the deer the princess killed a pricket.

sp.speaker: Nath.
sp.p: Perge, good Master Holofernes, perge; so it shall please you to abrogate scurrility.

sp.speaker: Hol.
sp.l: I will something affect the letter, for it argues facility.

The preyful princess pierced and prick'd a pretty
pleasing pricket;

Some say a sore; but not a sore, till now made
sore with shooting.

The dogs did yell; put L to sore, then sorel jumps
from thicket;

Or pricket sore, or else sorel; the people fall
a-hooting.

If sore be sore, then L to sore makes fifty sores
one sorel.

Of one sore I an hundred make by adding but
one more L.

sp.speaker: Nath.
sp.p: A rare talent!

sp.speaker: Dull.
sp.p: If a talent be a claw, look how he claws him with a talent.

sp.speaker: Hol.
sp.p: This is a gift that I have, simple, simple; a foolish extravagant spirit, full of forms, figures, shapes, objects, ideas, apprehensions, motions, revolutions: these are begot in the ventricle of memory, nourished in the womb of pia mater, and delivered upon the mellowing of occasion. But the gift is good in those in whom it is acute, and I am thankful for it.

sp.speaker: Nath.
sp.p: Sir, I praise the Lord for you: and so may my parishioners; for their sons are well tutored by you, and their daughters profit very greatly under you: you are a good member of the commonwealth.

sp.speaker: Hol.
sp.p:
Mehercle, if their sons be ingenuous, they shall want no instruction; if their daughters be capable, I will put it to them: but vir sapit qui pauca loquitur; a soul feminine saluteth us.
Enter JAQUENETTA and COSTARD.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: God give you good morrow, master Parson.

sp.speaker: Hol.
sp.p: Master Parson, quasi pers-on. An if one should be pierced, which is the one?

sp.speaker: Cost.
sp.p: Marry, master schoolmaster, he that is likest to a hogshead.

sp.speaker: Hol.
sp.p: Piercing a hogshead! a good lustre of conceit in a tuft of earth; fire enough for a flint, pearl enough for a swine: 'tis pretty; it is well.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.p: Good master Parson, be so good as read me this letter: it was given me by Costard, and sent me from Don Armado: I beseech you, read it.

sp.speaker: Hol.
sp.p: Fauste, precor gelida quando pecus omne sub umbra Ruminat,--and so forth. Ah, good old Mantuan! I may speak of thee as the traveller doth of Venice;
sp.l: Venetia, Venetia,
Chi non ti vede non ti pretia.
sp.p: Old Mantuan, old Mantuan! who understandeth thee not, loves thee not. Ut, re, sol, la, mi, fa. Under pardon, sir, what are the contents? or rather, as Horace says in his--What, my soul, verses?

sp.speaker: Nath.
sp.p: Ay, sir, and very learned.

sp.speaker: Hol.
sp.p: Let me hear a staff, a stanze, a verse; lege, domine.

sp.speaker: Nath.
sp.l:
If love make me forsworn, how shall I swear to
love?

Ah, never faith could hold, if not to beauty
vow'd!

Though to myself forsworn, to thee I'll faithful
prove;

Those thoughts to me were oaks, to thee like
osiers bow'd.

Study his bias leaves and makes his book thine
eyes,

Where all those pleasures live that art would
comprehend:

If knowledge be the mark, to know thee shall
suffice;

Well learned is that tongue that well can thee
commend,

All ignorant that soul that sees thee without
wonder;

Which is to me some praise that I thy parts
admire:

Thy eye Jove's lightning bears, thy voice his
dreadful thunder,

Which, not to anger bent, is music and sweet
fire.
Celestial as thou art, O, pardon, love, this wrong,

That sings heaven's praise with such an earthly
tongue.

sp.speaker: Hol.
sp.p: You find not the apostraphas, and so miss the accent: let me supervise the canzonet. Here are only numbers ratified; but, for the elegancy, facility, and golden cadence of poesy, caret. Ovidius Naso was the man: and why, indeed, Naso, but for smelling out the odoriferous flowers of fancy, the jerks of invention? Imitari is nothing: so doth the hound his master, the ape his keeper, the tired horse his rider. But, damosella virgin, was this directed to you?

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.p: Ay, sir, from one Monsieur Biron, one of the strange queen's lords.

sp.speaker: Hol.
sp.p: I will overglance the superscript: 'To the snow-white hand of the most beauteous Lady Rosaline.' I will look again on the intellect of the letter, for the nomination of the party writing to the person written unto: 'Your ladyship's in all desired employment, BIRON.' Sir Nathaniel, this Biron is one ofthe votaries with the king; and here he hath framed a letter to a sequent of the stranger queen's, which accidentally, or by the way of progression, hath miscarried. Trip and go, my sweet; deliver this paper into the royal hand of the king: it may concern much. Stay not thy compliment; I forgive thy duty: adieu.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Good Costard, go with me. Sir, God save your life!

sp.speaker: Cost.
sp.p:
Have with thee, my girl.
Exeunt Cost. and Jaq.

sp.speaker: Nath.
sp.p: Sir, you have done this in the fear of God, very religiously; and, as a certain father saith,--

sp.speaker: Hol.
sp.p: Sir, tell not me of the father; I do fear colorable colors. But to return to the verses: did they please you, Sir Nathaniel?

sp.speaker: Nath.
sp.p: Marvellous well for the pen.

sp.speaker: Hol.
sp.p: I do dine to-day at the father's of a certain pupil of mine; where, if, before repast, it shall please you to gratify the table with a grace, I will, on my privilege I have with the parents of the foresaid child or pupil, undertake your ben venuto; where I will prove those verses to be very unlearned, neither savouring of poetry, wit, nor invention: I beseech your society.

sp.speaker: Nath.
sp.p: And thank you too; for society, saith the text, is the happiness of life.

sp.speaker: Hol.
sp.p: And, certes, the text most infallibly concludes it.To DullSir, I do invite you too; you shall not say me nay: pauca verba. Away! the gentles are at their game, and we will to our recreation. Exeunt.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.p:
The king he is hunting the deer; I am coursing myself: they have pitched a toil; I am toiling in a pitch,--pitch that defiles: defile! a foul word. Well, set thee down, sorrow! for so they say the fool said, and so say I, and I the fool: well proved, wit! By the Lord, this love is as mad as Ajax: it kills sheep; it kills me, I a sheep: well proved again o' my side! I will not love: if I do, hang me; i' faith, I will not. O, but her eye,--by this light, but for her eye, I would not love her; yes, for her two eyes. Well, I do nothing in the world but lie, and lie in my throat. By heaven, I do love: and it hath taught me to rhyme and to be melancholy; and here is part of my rhyme, and here my melancholy. Well, she hath one o' my sonnets already: the clown bore it, the fool sent it, and the lady hath it: sweet clown, sweeter fool, sweetest lady! By the world, I would not care a pin, if the other three were in. Here comes one with a paper: God give him grace to groan! Stands aside.
Enter the King, with a paper.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: Ay, me!

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.p: Shot, by heaven! Proceed, sweet Cupid: thou hast thumped him with thy bird-bolt under the left pap. In faith, secrets!

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: So sweet a kiss the golden sun gives not
To those fresh morning drops upon the rose,

As thy eye-beams, when their fresh rays have
smote
The night of dew that on my cheeks down flows:
Nor shines the silver moon one half so bright
Through the transparent bosom of the deep,
As doth thy face through tears of mine give light;
Thou shinest in every tear that I do weep:
No drop but as a coach doth carry thee;
So ridest thou triumphing in my woe,
Do but behold the tears that swell in me,
And they thy glory through my grief will show:
But do not love thyself; then thou wilt keep
My tears for glasses, and still make me weep.
O queen of queens! how far dost thou excel,
No thought can think, nor tongue of mortal tell.

How shall she know my griefs? I'll drop the
paper:

Sweet leaves, shade folly. Who is he comes here?
Steps aside
What, Longaville! and reading! listen, ear.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l:
Now, in thy likeness, one more fool
appear!
Enter LONGAVILLE, with a paper.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.p: Ay me, I am forsworn!

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.p: Why, he comes in like a perjure, wearing papers.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l:
In love, I hope: sweet fellowship in
shame!

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l:
One drunkard loves another of the
name.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l:
Am I the first that have been
perjured so?

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l:
I could put thee in comfort. Not by
two that I know:

Thou makest the triumviry, the corner-cap of
society,

The shape of Love's Tyburn that hangs up
simplicity.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l:
I fear these stubborn lines lack power
to move.
O sweet Maria, empress of my love!
These numbers will I tear, and write in prose.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l:
O, rhymes are guards on wanton
Cupid's hose:
Disfigure not his slop.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: This same shall go. Reads.
Did not the heavenly rhetoric of thine eye,
'Gainst whom the world cannot hold argument,
Persuade my heart to this false perjury?
Vows for thee broke deserve not punishment.
A woman I forswore; but I will prove,
Thou being a goddess, I forswore not thee:
My vow was earthly, thou a heavenly love;
Thy grace being gain'd cures all disgrace in me.
Vows are but breath, and breath a vapour is:

Then thou, fair sun, which on my earth dost
shine,
Exhalest this vapour-vow; in thee it is:
If broken then, it is no fault of mine:
If by me broke, what fool is not so wise
To lose an oath to win a paradise?

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l:
This is the liver-vein, which makes
flesh a deity,
A green goose a goddess: pure, pure idolatry.

God amend us, God amend! we are much out o'
the way.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l:
By whom shall I send
this?--Company! stay. Steps aside.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l: All hid, all hid; an old infant play.
Like a demigod here sit I in the sky,
And wretched fools' secrets heedfully o'er-eye.

More sacks to the mill! O heavens, I have my
wish!
Enter DUMAIN, with a paper.
Dumain transform'd! four woodcocks in a dish!

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.l: O most divine Kate!

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l: O most profane coxcomb!

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.l: By heaven, the wonder in a mortal eye!

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l:
By earth, she is not, corporal, there
you lie.

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.l:
Her amber hair for foul hath amber
quoted.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l:
An amber-colour'd raven was well
noted.

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.l: As upright as the cedar.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l: Stoop, I say;
Her shoulder is with child.

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.l: As fair as day.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l:
Ay, as some days; but then no sun
must shine.

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.l: O that I had my wish!

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: And I had mine!

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: And I mine too, good Lord!

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l:
Amen, so I had mine: is not that a
good word?

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.l: I would forget her; but a fever she
Reigns in my blood and will remember'd be.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l:
A fever in your blood! why, then
incision
Would let her out in saucers: sweet misprision!

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.l:
Once more I'll read the ode that I
have writ.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l:
Once more I'll mark how love can
vary wit.

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.l: On a day--alack the day!--
Love, whose month is ever May,
Spied a blossom passing fair
Playing in the wanton air:
Through the velvet leaves the wind,
All unseen, can passage find;
That the lover, sick to death,
Wish himself the heaven's breath.
Air, quoth he, thy cheeks may blow;
Air, would I might triumph so!
But, alack, my hand is sworn
Ne'er to pluck thee from thy thorn;
Vow, alack, for youth unmeet,
Youth so apt to pluck a sweet!
Do not call it sin in me,
That I am forsworn for thee;
Thou for whom Jove would swear
Juno but an Ethiope were;
And deny himself for Jove,
Turning mortal for thy love.
This will I send and something else more plain,
That shall express my true love's fasting pain.
O, would the king, Biron, and Longaville,
Were lovers too! Ill, to example ill,
Would from my forehead wipe a perjured note;
For none offend where all alike do dote.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l:
Dumain, thy love is far
from charity,
That in love's grief desirest society:
You may look pale, but I should blush, I know,
To be o'erheard and taken napping so.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l:
Come, sir, you blush; as
his your case is such;
You chide at him, offending twice as much;
You do not love Maria; Longaville
Did never sonnet for her sake compile,
Nor never lay his wreathed arms athwart
His loving bosom to keep down his heart.
I have been closely shrouded in this bush
And mark'd you both and for you both did blush:
I heard your guilty rhymes, observed your fashion,
Saw sighs reek from you, noted well your passion:
Ay me! says one; Jove! the other cries;
One, her hairs were gold, crystal the other's eyes: To Long.

You would for paradise break faith
and troth; To Dum.

And Jove, for your love, would
infringe an oath.
What will Biron say when that he shall hear
Faith so infringed, which such zeal did swear?
How will he scorn! how will he spend his wit!
How will he triumph, leap and laugh at it!
For all the wealth that ever I did see,
I would not have him know so much by me.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l: Now step I forth to whip hypocrisy. Advancing.
Ah, good my liege, I pray thee, pardon me!
Good heart, what grace hast thou, thus to reprove
These worms for loving, that art most in love?
Your eyes do make no coaches; in your tears
There is no certain princess that appears;
You'll not be perjured, 'tis a hateful thing;
Tush, none but minstrels like of sonneting!
But are you not ashamed? nay, are you not,
All three of you, to be thus much o'ershot?
You found his mote; the king your mote did see;
But I a beam do find in each of three.
O, what a scene of foolery have I seen,
Of sighs, of groans, of sorrow and of teen!
O me, with what strict patience have I sat,
To see a king transformed to a gnat!
To see great Hercules whipping a gig,
And profound Solomon to tune a jig,
And Nestor play at push-pin with the boys,
And critic Timon laugh at idle toys!
Where lies thy grief, O, tell me, good Dumain?
And, gentle Longaville, where lies thy pain?
And where my liege's? all about the breast:
A caudle, ho!

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Too bitter is thy jest.
Are we betray'd thus to thy over-view?

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l: Not you to me, but I betray'd by you:
I, that am honest; I, that hold it sin
To break the vow I am engaged in;
I am betray'd, by keeping company
With men like men of inconstancy.
When shall you see me write a thing in rhyme?
Or groan for love? or spend a minute's time
In pruning me? When shall you hear that I
Will praise a hand, a foot, a face, an eye,
A gait, a state, a brow, a breast, a waist,
A leg, a limb?

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Soft! whither away so fast
A true man or a thief that gallops so?

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l:
I post from love: good lover, let me go.
Enter JAQUENETTA and COSTARD.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: God bless the king!

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: What present hast thou there?

sp.speaker: Cost.
sp.l: Some certain treason.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: What makes treason here?

sp.speaker: Cost.
sp.l: Nay, it makes nothing, sir.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: If it mar nothing neither,
The treason and you go in peace away together.

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l:
I beseech your grace, let this letter
be read:
Our parson misdoubts it; 'twas treason, he said.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l:
Biron, read it over.
Giving him the paper.
Where hadst thou it?

sp.speaker: Jaq.
sp.l: Of Costard.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Where hadst thou it ?

sp.speaker: Cost.
sp.l:
Of Dun Adramadio, Dun Adramadio.
Biron tears the letter.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l:
How now! what is in you? why dost
thou tear it?

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l:
A toy, my liege, a toy: your grace
needs not fear it.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l:
It did move him to passion, and
therefore let's hear it.

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.l:
It is Biron's writing, and here is his
name. Gathering up the pieces.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l:
Ah, you whoreson
loggerhead! you were born to do me shame.
Guilty, my lord, guilty! I confess, I confess.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: What?

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l:
That you three fools lack'd me fool to
make up the mess:
He, he, and you, and you, my liege, and I,
Are pick-purses in love, and we deserve to die.
O, dismiss this audience, and I shall tell you more.

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.l: Now the number is even.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l: True, true; we are four.
Will these turtles be gone?

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Hence, sirs; away!

sp.speaker: Cost.
sp.l:
Walk aside the true folk, and let the
traitors stay.
Exeunt Costard and Jaquenetta.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l:
Sweet lords, sweet lovers, O, let us
embrace!
As true we are as flesh and blood can be:
The sea will ebb and flow, heaven show his face;
Young blood doth not obey an old decree:
We cannot cross the cause why we were born;
Therefore of all hands must we be forsworn.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l:
What, did these rent lines show some
love of thine?

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l:
Did they, quoth you? Who sees the
heavenly Rosaline,
That, like a rude and savage man of Inde,
At the first opening of the gorgeous east,
Bows not his vassal head and strucken blind
Kisses the base ground with obedient breast?
