What peremptory eagle-sighted eye
Dares look upon the heaven of her brow,
That is not blinded by her majesty?

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l:
What zeal, what fury hath inspired thee
now?
My love, her mistress, is a gracious moon;
She an attending star, scarce seen a light.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l: My eyes are then no eyes, nor I Biron:
O, but for my love, day would turn to night!
Of all complexions the cull'd sovereignty
Do meet, as at a fair, in her fair cheek,
Where several worthies make one dignity,
Where nothing wants that want itself doth seek.
Lend me the flourish of all gentle tongues,--
Fie, painted rhetoric! O, she needs it not:
To things of sale a seller's praise belongs,

She passes praise; then praise too short doth
blot.
A wither'd hermit, five-score winters worn,
Might shake off fifty, looking in her eye:
Beauty doth varnish age, as if new-born,
And gives the crutch the cradle's infancy:
O, 'tis the sun that maketh all things shine.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: By heaven, thy love is black as ebony.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l: Is ebony like her? O wood divine!
A wife of such wood were felicity.
O, who can give an oath? where is a book?
That I may swear beauty doth beauty lack,
If that she learn not of her eye to look:
No face is fair that is not full so black.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: O paradox ! Black is the badge of hell,
The hue of dungeons and the suit of night;
And beauty's crest becomes the heavens well.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l:
Devils soonest tempt, resembling spirits
of light.
O, if in black my lady's brows be deck'd,
It mourns that painting and usurping hair
Should ravish doters with a false aspect;
And therefore is she born to make black fair.
Her favour turns the fashion of the days,
For native blood is counted painting now;
And therefore red, that would avoid dispraise,
Paints itself black, to imitate her brow.

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.l:
To look like her are chimney-sweepers
black.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l:
And since her time are colliers counted
bright.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l:
And Ethiopes of their sweet complexion
crack.

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.l:
Dark needs no candles now, for dark is
light.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l: Your mistresses dare never come in rain,
For fear their colours should be wash'd away.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l:
'Twere good, yours did; for, sir, to tell
you plain,
I'll find a fairer face not wash'd to-day.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l:
I'll prove her fair, or talk till doomsday
here.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l:
No devil will fright thee then so much
as she.

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.l: I never knew man hold vile stuff so dear.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l:
Look, here's thy love: my foot and her
face see.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l:
O, if the streets were paved with thine
eyes,
Her feet were much too dainty for such tread!

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.l:
O vile! then, as she goes, what upward
lies
The street should see as she walk'd overhead.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: But what of this? are we not all in love?

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l:
Nothing so sure; and thereby all
forsworn.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l:
Then leave this chat; and, good Biron,
now prove
Our loving lawful, and our faith not torn.

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.l:
Ay, marry, there; some flattery for this
evil.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: O, some authority how to proceed;
Some tricks, some quillets, how to cheat the devil.

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.l: Some salve for perjury.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l: 'Tis more than need.
Have at you, then, affection's men at arms.
Consider what you first did swear unto,
To fast, to study, and to see no woman;
Flat treason 'gainst the kingly state of youth.
Say, can you fast? your stomachs are too young;
And abstinence engenders maladies.
And where that you have vow'd to study, lords,
In that each of you have forsworn his book,
Can you still dream and pore and thereon look?
For when would you, my lord, or you, or you,
Have found the ground of study's excellence
Without the beauty of a woman's face?
[From women's eyes this doctrine I derive;
They are the ground, the books, the academes

From whence doth spring the true Promethean
fire.]
Why, universal plodding poisons up
The nimble spirits in the arteries,
As motion and long-during action tires
The sinewy vigor of the traveller.
Now, for not looking on a woman's face,
You have in that forsworn the use of eyes
And study too, the causer of your vow;
For where is any author in the world
Teaches such beauty as a woman's eye?
Learning is but an adjunct to ourself
And where we are our learning likewise is:
Then when ourselves we see in ladies' eyes,
Do we not likewise see our learning there?
O, we have made a vow to study, lords,
And in that vow we have forsworn our books.
For when would you, my liege, or you, or you,
In leaden contemplation have found out
Such fiery numbers as the prompting eyes
Of beauty's tutors have enrich'd you with ?
Other slow arts entirely keep the brain;
And therefore, finding barren practisers,
Scarce show a harvest of their heavy toil:
But love, first learned in a lady's eyes,
Lives not alone immured in the brain;
But, with the motion of all elements,
Courses as swift as thought in every power,
And gives to every power a double power,
Above their functions and their offices.
It adds a precious seeing to the eye;
A lover's eyes will gaze an eagle blind;
A lover's ear will hear the lowest sound,
When the suspicious head of theft is stopp'd:
Love's feeling is more soft and sensible
Than are the tender horns of cockled snails;

Love's tongue proves dainty Bacchus gross in
taste:
For valour, is not Love a Hercules,
Still climbing trees in the Hesperides?
Subtle as Sphinx; as sweet and musical
As bright Apollo's lute, strung with his hair:

And when Love speaks, the voice of all the
gods
Makes heaven drowsy with the harmony.
Never durst poet touch a pen to write
Until his ink were temper'd with Love's sighs;
O, then his lines would ravish savage ears
And plant in tyrants mild humility.
From women's eyes this doctrine I derive:
They sparkle still the right Promethean fire;
They are the books, the arts, the academes,
That show, contain and nourish all the world:
Else none at all in aught proves excellent.
Then fools you were these women to forswear,
Or keeping what is sworn, you will prove fools.
For wisdom's sake, a word that all men love,
Or for love's sake, a word that loves all men,
Or for men's sake, the authors of these women,
Or women's sake, by whom we men are men,
Let us once lose our oaths to find ourselves,
Or else we lose ourselves to keep our oaths,
It is religion to be thus forsworn,
For charity itself fulfils the law,
And who can sever love from charity?

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l:
Saint Cupid, then! and, soldiers, to the
field !

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l:
Advance your standards, and upon
them, lords;
Pell-mell, down with them! but be first advised,
In conflict that you get the sun of them.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Now to plain-dealing; lay these glozes by:
Shall we resolve to woo these girls of France?

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l:
And win them too: therefore let us
devise
Some entertainment for them in their tents.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l:
First, from the park let us conduct
them thither;
Then homeward every man attach the hand
Of his fair mistress: in the afternoon
We will with some strange pastime solace them,
Such as the shortness of the time can shape;
For revels, dances, masks and merry hours
Forerun fair Love, strewing her way with flowers.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Away, away! no time shall be omitted
That will betime, and may by us be fitted.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l:
Allons! allons! Sow'd cockle reap'd no
corn;
And justice always whirls in equal measure:

Light wenches may prove plagues to men
forsworn;
If so, our copper buys no better treasure. Exeunt.

div.head: SCENE I
div.stage:
Enter HOLOFERNES, SIR NATHANIEL, and
DULL.

sp.speaker: Hol.
sp.l: Satis quod sufficit.

sp.speaker: Nath.
sp.p: I praise God for you, sir: your reasons at dinner have been sharp and sententious: pleasant without scurrility, witty, with- out affection, audacious without impudency, learned without opinion, and strange without heresy. I did converse this quondam day with a companion of the king's, who is intituled, nominated or called, Don Adriano de Armado.

sp.speaker: Hol.
sp.p: Novi hominem tanquam te: his humor is lofty, his discourse peremptory, his tongue filed, his eye ambitious, his gait majestical, and his general behavior vain, ridiculous, and thrasonical. He is too picked, too spruce, too affected, too odd, as it were, too peregrinate, as I may call it.

sp.speaker: Nath.
sp.l:
A most singular and choice epithet.
Draws out his table-book.

sp.speaker: Hol.
sp.p: He draweth out the thread of his verbosity finer than the staple of his argument. I abhor such fanatical phantasimes, such insociable and point-devise companions; such rackers of orthography, as to speak dout, fine, when he should say doubt; det, when he should pronounce debt,--d, e, b, t, not d, e, t: he clepeth a calf, cauf; half, hauf; neighbor vocatur nebour; neigh abbreviated ne. This is abhominable,--which he would call abbominable: it insinuateth me of insanie: anne intelligis, domine? to make frantic, lunatic.

sp.speaker: Nath.
sp.l: Laus Deo, bene intelligo.

sp.speaker: Hol.
sp.p: Bon, bon, fort bon! Priscian a little scratched, 'twill serve.

sp.speaker: Nath.
sp.p: Videsne quis venit?

sp.speaker: Hol.
sp.l:
Video, et gaudeo.
Enter ARMADO, MOTH, and COSTARD.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.l: Chirrah ! To Moth.

sp.speaker: Hol.
sp.l: Quare chirrah, not sirrah?

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.l: Men of peace, well encountered.

sp.speaker: Hol.
sp.l: Most military sir, salutation.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: They have been at a great feast of languages, and stolen the scraps.

sp.speaker: Cost.
sp.p: O, they have lived long on the alms- basket of words. I marvel thy master hath not eaten thee for a word; for thou art not so long by the head as honorificabilitudinitatibus: thou art easier swallowed than a flap- dragon.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: Peace! the peal begins.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.l: Monsieur, are you not lettered?

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: Yes, yes;he teaches boys the hornbook. What is a, b, spelt backward, with the horn on his head?

sp.speaker: Hol.
sp.l: Ba, pueritia, with a horn added.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: Ba, most silly sheep with a horn. You hear his learning.

sp.speaker: Hol.
sp.p: Quis, quis, thou consonant?

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: The third of the five vowels, if you repeat them; or the fifth, if I.

sp.speaker: Hol.
sp.p: I will repeat them,--a, e, i,--

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: The sheep: the other two concludes it,--o, u.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.p: Now, by the salt wave of the Mediterraneum, a sweet touch, a quick venue of wit! snip, snap, quick and home! it rejoiceth my intellect: true wit!

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: Offered by a child to an old man; which is wit-old.

sp.speaker: Hol.
sp.p: What is the figure? what is the figure?

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: Horns.

sp.speaker: Hol.
sp.p: Thou disputest like an infant; go, whip thy gig.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: Lend me your horn to make one, and I will whip about your infamy circum circa,--a gig of a cuckold's horn.

sp.speaker: Cost.
sp.p: An I had but one penny in the world,thou shouldst have it to buy gingerbread: hold, there is the very remuneration I had of thy master, thou halfpenny purse of wit, thou pigeon-egg of discretion. O, an the heavens were so pleased that thou wert but my bastard, what a joyful father wouldst thou make me! Go to; thou hast it ad dunghill, at the fingers' ends, as they say.

sp.speaker: Hol.
sp.p: O, I smell false Latin; dunghill for unguem.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.p: Arts-man, preambulate, we will be singuled from the barbarous. Do you not educate youth at the charge-house on the top of the mountain?

sp.speaker: Hol.
sp.p: Or mons, the hill.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.p: At your sweet pleasure, for the mountain.

sp.speaker: Hol.
sp.l: I do, sans question.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.p: Sir, it is the king's most sweet pleasure and affection to congratulate the princess at her pavilion in the posteriors of this day, which the rude multitude call the afternoon.

sp.speaker: Hol.
sp.p: The posterior of the day, most generous sir, is liable, congruent and measurable for the afternoon: the word is well culled, chose, sweet and apt, I do assure you, sir, I do assure.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.p: Sir, the king is a noble gentleman, and my familiar, I do assure ye, very good friend: for what is inward between us, let it pass. I do beseech thee, remember thy courtesy; I beseech thee, apparel thy head: and among other important and most serious designs, and of great import indeed, too, but let that pass: for I must tell thee, it will please his grace, by the world, sometime to lean upon my poor shoulder, and with his royal finger, thus, dally with my excrement, with my mustachio; but, sweet heart, let that pass. By the world, I recount no fable: some certain special honors it pleaseth his greatness to impart to Armado, a soldier, a man of travel, that hath seen the world; but let that pass. The very all of all is,--but, sweet heart, I do implore secrecy,--that the king would have me present the princess, sweet chuck, with some delightful ostentation, or show, or pageant, or antique, or firework. Now, understanding that the curate and your sweet self are good at such eruptions and sudden breaking out of mirth, as it were, I have acquainted you withal, to the end to crave your assistance.

sp.speaker: Hol.
sp.p: Sir, you shall present before her the Nine Worthies. Sir, as concerning some entertainment of time, some show in the posterior of this day, to be rendered by our assistants, at the king's command, and this most gallant, illustrate, and learned gentleman, before the princess; I say none so fit as to present the Nine Worthies.

sp.speaker: Nath.
sp.p: Where will you find men worthy enough to present them?

sp.speaker: Hol.
sp.p: Joshua, yourself; myself and this gallant gentleman, Judas Maccabaeus; this swain, because of his great limb or joint, shall pass Pompey the Great; the page, Hercules,--

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.p: Pardon, sir ; error: he is not quantity enough for that Worthy's thumb: he is not so big as the end of his club.

sp.speaker: Hol.
Moth.
sp.p: An excellent device! so, if any of the audience hiss, you may cry 'Well done, Hercules! now thou crushest the snake!' that is the way to make an offence gracious, though few have the grace to do it.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.p: For the rest of the Worthies?--

sp.speaker: Hol.
sp.l: I will play three myself.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: Thrice-worthy gentleman!

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.p: Shall I tell you a thing?

sp.speaker: Hol.
sp.p: We attend.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.p: We will have, if this fadge not, an antique. I beseech you, follow.

sp.speaker: Hol.
sp.p: Via, goodman Dull! thou hast spoken no word all this while.

sp.speaker: Dull.
sp.p: Nor understood none neither, sir.

sp.speaker: Hol.
sp.l: Allons! we will employ thee.

sp.speaker: Dull.
sp.l:
I'll make one in a dance, or so; or I
will play

On the tabor to the Worthies, and let them
dance the hay.

sp.speaker: Hol.
sp.l:
Most dull, honest Dull! To our sport
away! Exeunt.

div.head: SCENE II
div.stage:
Enter the Princess, KATHARINE, ROSALINE,
and MARIA.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l:
Sweet hearts, we shall be rich ere we
depart,
If fairings come thus plentifully in:
A lady wall'd about witth diamonds!
Look you what I have from the loving king.

sp.speaker: Ros.
sp.l:
Madame, came nothing else along with
that?

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l:
Nothing but this! yes, as much love in
rhyme
As would be cramm'd up in a sheet of paper,
Writ o' both sides the leaf, margent and all,
That he was fain to seal on Cupid's name.

sp.speaker: Ros.
sp.l:
That was the way to make his godhead
wax,
For he hath been five thousand years a boy,

sp.speaker: Kath.
sp.l: Ay, and a shrewd unhappy gallows too.

sp.speaker: Ros.
sp.l:
You'll ne'er be friends with him; a' kill'd
your sister.

sp.speaker: Kath.
sp.l:
He made her melancholy, sad, and
heavy;
And so she died: had she been light, like you,
Of such a merry, nimble, stirring spirit,
She might ha' been a grandam ere she died:
And so may you; for a light heart lives long.

sp.speaker: Ros.
sp.l:
What's your dark meaning, mouse, of this
light word?

sp.speaker: Kath.
sp.l: A light condition in a beauty dark.

sp.speaker: Ros.
sp.l:
We need more light to find your meaning
out.

sp.speaker: Kath.
sp.l: You'll mar the light by taking it in snuff;
Therefore I'll darkly end the argument.

sp.speaker: Ros.
sp.l:
Look, what you do, you do it still i' the
dark.

sp.speaker: Kath.
sp.l: So do not you, for you are a light wench.

sp.speaker: Ros.
sp.l:
Indeed I weigh not you, and therefore
light.

sp.speaker: Kath.
sp.l:
You weigh me not? O, that's you care
not for me.

sp.speaker: Ros.
sp.l:
Great reason; for 'past cure is still past
care.'

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l:
Well bandied both; a set of wit well
play'd.
But, Rosaline, you have a favor too:
Who sent it? and what is it?

sp.speaker: Ros.
sp.l: I would you knew:
An if my face were but as fair as yours,
My favour were as great: be witness this.
Nay, I have verses too, I thank Biron:
The numbers true; and, were the numbering too,
I were the fairest goddess on the ground:
I am compared to twenty thousand fairs,
O, he hath drawn my picture in his letter!

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l: Any thing like?

sp.speaker: Ros.
sp.l: Much in the letters; nothing in the praise.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l: Beauteous as ink; a good conclusion.

sp.speaker: Kath.
sp.l: Fair as a text B in a copy-book.

sp.speaker: Ros.
sp.l:
'Ware pencils, ho! let me not die your
debtor,
My red dominical, my golden letter:
O that your face were not so full of O's!

sp.speaker: Kath.
sp.l:
A pox of that jest! and I beshrew all
shrows.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l:
But, Katharine, what was sent to you
from fair Dumain?

sp.speaker: Kath.
sp.l: Madam, this glove.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l: Did he not send you twain?

sp.speaker: Kath.
sp.l: Yes, madam, and moreover
Some thousand verses of a faithful lover,
A huge translation of hypocrisy,
Vilely compiled, profound simplicity.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l:
This and these pearls to me sent
Longaville:
The letter is too long by half a mile.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l:
I think no less. Dost thou not wish in
heart
The chain were longer and the letter short?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l:
Ay, or I would these hands might never
part.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l: We are wise girls to mock our lovers so.

sp.speaker: Ros.
sp.l:
They are worse fools to purchase
mocking so.
That same Biron I'll torture ere I go:
O that I knew he were but in by the week!
How I would make him fawn and beg and seek
And wait the season and observe the times
And spend his prodigal wits in bootless rhymes
And shape his service wholly to my hests
And make him proud to make me proud that jests!
So perttaunt-like would I o'ersway his state
That he should be my fool and I his fate.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l:
None are so surely caught, when they
are catch'd,
As wit turn'd fool: folly, in wisdom hatch'd.
Hath wisdom's warrant and the help of school
And wit's own grace to grace a learned fool.

sp.speaker: Ros.
sp.l:
The blood of youth burns not with such
excess
As gravity's revolt to wantonness.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Folly in fools bears not so strong a note
As foolery in the wise, when wit doth dote;
Since all the power thereof it doth apply
To prove, by wit, worth in simplicity.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l:
Here comes Boyet, and mirth is in his
face.
Enter BOYET.

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.l:
O, I am stabb'd with laughter! Where's
her grace?

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l: Thy news, Boyet?

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.l: Prepare, madam, prepare!
Arm, wenches, arm! encounters mounted are

Against your peace: Love doth approach
disguised,
Armed in arguments; you'll be surprised:
Muster your wits; stand in your own defence;
Or hide your heads like cowards, and fly hence.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l:
Saint Denis to Saint Cupid! What are
they

That charge their breath against us? say, scout,
say.

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.l: Under the cool shade of a sycamore
I thought to close mine eyes some half an hour;
When, lo! to interrupt my purposed rest,
Toward that shade I might behold addrest
The king and his companions: warily
I stole into a neighbour thicket by,
And overheard what you shall overhear,
That, by and by, disguised they will be here.
Their herald is a pretty knavish page,
That well by heart hath conn'd his embassage:
Action and accent did they teach him there;
'Thus must thou speak,' and 'thus thy body bear:'
And ever and anon they made a doubt
Presence majestical would put him out;
'For,' quoth the king, 'an angel shalt thou see;
Yet fear not thou, but speak audaciously.'
The boy replied, 'An angel is not evil;
I should have fear'd her had she been a devil.'

With that, all laugh'd and clapp'd him on the
shoulder,
Making the bold wag by their praises bolder:
One rubb'd his elbow thus, and fleer'd and swore
A better speech was never spoke before;
Another, with his finger and his thumb,
Cried, 'Via! we will do't, come what will come;'
The third he caper'd, and cried, 'All goes well;'
The fourth turn'd on the toe, and down he fell.
With that, they all did tumble on the ground,
With such a zealous laughter, so profound,
That in this spleen ridiculous appears,
To check their folly, passion's solemn tears.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l:
But what, but what, come they to visit
us?

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.l:
They do, they do; and are apparell'd
thus,
Like Muscovites or Russians, as I guess.
Their purpose is to parle, to court and dance;
And every one his love-feat will advance
Unto his several mistress, which they'll know
By favors several which they did bestow.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l:
And will they so? the gallants shall be
task'd;
For, ladies, we will every one be mask'd;
And not a man of them shall have the grace,
Despite of suit, to see a lady's face.
Hold, Rosaline, this favour thou shalt wear,
And then the king will court thee for his dear;
Hold, take thou this, my sweet, and give me thine,
So shall Biron take me for Rosaline.
And change you favors too; so shall your loves
Woo contrary, deceived by these removes.

sp.speaker: Ros.
sp.l:
Come on, then; wear the favours most
in sight.

sp.speaker: Kath.
sp.l: But in this changing what is your intent?

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l: The effect of my intent is to cross theirs:
They do it but in mocking merriment;
And mock for mock is only my intent.
Their several counsels they unbosom shall
To loves mistook, and so be mock'd withal
Upon the next occasion that we meet,
With visages display'd, to talk and greet.

sp.speaker: Ros.
sp.l: But shall we dance, if they desire us to 't?

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l: No, to the death, we will not move a foot;
Nor to their penn'd speech render we no grace,
But while 'tis spoke each turn away her face.

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.l:
Why, that contempt will kill the
speaker's heart,
And quite divorce his memory from his part.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l: Therefore I do it; and I make no doubt
The rest will ne'er come in, if he be out
There's no such sport as sport by sport o'erthrown,
To make theirs ours and ours none but our own:
So shall we stay, mocking intended game,

And they, well mock'd, depart away with shame.
Trumpets sound within.

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.l:
The trumpet sounds: be mask'd; the
maskers come. The Ladies mask.
Enter Blackamoors with music; MOTH; the
King, BIRON, LONGAVILLE, and DUMAIN, in
Russian habits, and masked.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.l:
All hail, the richest beauties on the
earth!--

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.l: Beauties no richer than rich taffeta.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.l:
A holy parcel of the fairest dames
The Ladies turn their backs to him.
That ever turn'd their--backs--to mortal views!

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l:
Their eyes, villain,
their eyes.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.l:
That ever turn'd their eyes to mortal
views!--
Out--

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.l: True; out indeed.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.l:
Out of your favors, heavenly spirits,
vouchsafe
Not to behold--

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l: Once to behold, rogue.

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.l:
Once to behold with your sun-beamed
eyes,
--with your sun-beamed eyes--

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.l: They will not answer to that epithet;
You were best call it 'daughter-beamed eyes.'

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.l:
They do not mark me, and that brings
me out.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l:
Is this your perfectness? be gone, you
rogue! Exit Moth.

sp.speaker: Ros.
sp.l:
What would these strangers? know their
minds, Boyet:
If they do speak our language, 'tis our will
That some plain man recount their purposes:
Know what they would.

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.l: What would you with the princess?

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l: Nothing but peace and gentle visitation.

sp.speaker: Ros.
sp.l: What would they, say they?

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.l: Nothing but peace and gentle visitation.

sp.speaker: Ros.
sp.l:
Why, that they have; and bid them so
be gone.

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.l:
She says, you have it, and you may be
gone.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l:
Say to her, we have measured many
miles
To tread a measure with her on this grass.

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.l:
They say, that they have measured
many a mile
To tread a measure with you on this grass.

sp.speaker: Ros.
sp.l: It is not so. Ask them how many inches
Is in one mile: if they have measured many,
The measure then of one is easily told.

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.l:
If to come hither you have measured
miles,
And many miles, the princess bids you tell
How many inches doth fill up one mile.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l:
Tell her, we measure them by weary
steps.

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.l: She hears herself.

sp.speaker: Ros.
sp.l: How many weary steps,
Of many weary miles you have o'ergone,
Are number'd in the travel of one mile?

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l:
We number nothing that we spend for
you:
Our duty is so rich, so infinite,
That we may do it still without accompt.
Vouchsafe to show the sunshine of your face,
That we, like savages, may worship it.

sp.speaker: Ros.
sp.l: My face is but a moon, and clouded too.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l:
Blessed are clouds, to do as such clouds
do!

Vouchsafe, bright moon, and these thy stars, to
shine,
Those clouds removed, upon our watery eyne.

sp.speaker: Ros.
sp.l: O vain petitioner! beg a greater matter;
Thou now request'st but moonshine in the water.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l:
Then, in our measure do but vouchsafe
one change.
Thou bid'st me beg: this begging is not strange.

sp.speaker: Ros.
sp.l:
Play, music, then! Nay, you must do
it soon. Music plays.

Not yet! no dance! Thus change I like the
moon.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l:
Will you not dance? How come you
thus estranged?

sp.speaker: Ros.
sp.l:
You took the moon at full, but now she's
changed.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Yet still she is the moon, and I the man.
The music plays; vouchsafe some motion to it.

sp.speaker: Ros.
sp.l: Our ears vouchsafe it.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: But your legs should do it.

sp.speaker: Ros.
sp.l:
Since you are strangers and come here
by chance,

We'll not be nice: take hands. We will not
dance.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Why take we hands, then?

sp.speaker: Ros.
sp.l: Only to part friends:
Curtsy, sweet hearts; and so the measure ends.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l:
More measure of this measure; be not
nice.

sp.speaker: Ros.
sp.l: We can afford no more at such a price.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l:
Prize you yourselves: what buys your
company?

sp.speaker: Ros.
sp.l: Your absence only.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: That can never be.

sp.speaker: Ros.
sp.l:
Then cannot we be bought: and so,
adieu;
Twice to your visor, and half once to you.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l:
If you deny to dance, let's hold more
chat.

sp.speaker: Ros.
sp.l: In private, then.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l:
I am best pleased with that.
They converse apart.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l:
White-handed mistress, one sweet word
with thee.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l:
Honey, and milk, and sugar; there is
three.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l:
Nay then, two treys, and if you grow
so nice,
Metheglin, wort, and malmsey: well run, dice!
There's half a dozen sweets.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l: Seventh sweet, adieu:
Since you can cog, I'll play no more with you.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l: One word in secret.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l: Let it not be sweet.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l: Thou grievest my gall.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l: Gall! bitter.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l:
Therefore meet.
They converse apart.

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.l:
Will you vouchsafe with me to change
a word?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Name it.

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.l: Fair lady,--

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Say you so? Fair lord,--
Take that for your fair lady.

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.l: Please it you,

As much in private, and I'll bid adieu.
They converse apart.

sp.speaker: Kath.
sp.l:
What, was your vizard made without
a tongue?

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: I know the reason, lady, why you ask.

sp.speaker: Kath.
sp.l: O for your reason! quickly, sir; I long.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l:
You have a double tongue within your
mask,
And would afford my speechless vizard half.

sp.speaker: Kath.
sp.l:
Veal, quoth the Dutchman. Is not
'veal' a calf?

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: A calf, fair lady!

sp.speaker: Kath.
sp.l: No, a fair lord calf.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Let's part the word.

sp.speaker: Kath.
sp.l: No, I'll not be your half:
Take all, and wean it; it may prove an ox.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l:
Look, how you butt yourself in these
sharp mocks!
Will you give horns, chaste lady? do not so.

sp.speaker: Kath.
sp.l:
Then die a calf, before your horns do
grow.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: One word in private with you, ere I die.

sp.speaker: Kath.
sp.l:
Bleat softly then; the butcher hears
you cry. They converse apart.

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.l:
The tongues of mocking wenches are
as keen
As is the razor's edge invisible.
Cutting a smaller hair than may be seen,
Above the sense of sense; so sensible

Seemeth their conference; their conceits have
wings

Fleeter than arrows, bullets, wind, thought,
swifter things.

sp.speaker: Ros.
sp.l:
Not one word more, my maids; break
off, break off.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l:
By heaven, all dry-beaten with pure
scoff!

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l:
Farewell, mad wenches; You have
simple wits.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l:
Twenty adieus, my frozen Muscovits.
Exeunt King, Lords, and Blackamoors.
Are these the breed of wits so wonder'd at?

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.l:
Tapers they are, with your sweet
breaths puff'd out.

sp.speaker: Ros.
sp.l:
Well-liking wits they have; gross, gross;
fat, fat.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l: O poverty in wit, kingly-poor flout!

Will they not, think you, hang themselves
tonight?
Or ever, but in vizards, show their faces?
This pert Biron was out of countenance quite.

sp.speaker: Ros.
sp.l: O, they were all in lamentable cases!
The king was weeping-ripe for a good word.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l: Biron did swear himself out of all suit.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Dumain was at my service, and his sword:

No point, quoth I; my servant straight was
mute.

sp.speaker: Kath.
sp.l:
Lord Longaville said, I came o'er his
heart;
And trow you what he call'd me?

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l: Qualm, perhaps.

sp.speaker: Kath.
sp.l: Yes, in good faith.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l: Go, sickness as thou art!

sp.speaker: Ros.
sp.l:
Well, better wits have worn plain
statute-caps.
But will you hear? the king is my love sworn.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l:
And quick Biron hath plighted faith
to me.

sp.speaker: Kath.
sp.l: And Longaville was for my service born.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: Dumain is mine, as sure as bark on tree.

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.l:
Madam, and pretty mistresses, give
ear:
Immediately they will again be here
In their own shapes; for it can never be
They will digest this harsh indignity.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l: Will they return?

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.l: They will, they will, God knows,
And leap for joy, though they are lame with blows:
Therefore change favors; and, when they repair,
Blow like sweet roses in this summer air.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l:
How blow? how blow? speak to be
understood.

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.l:
Fair ladies mask'd are roses in their
bud;

Dismask'd, their damask sweet commixture
shown,
Are angels vailing clouds, or roses blown.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l: Avaunt, perplexity! What shall we do,
If they return in their own shapes to woo?

sp.speaker: Ros.
sp.l: Good madam, if by me you'll be advised,
Let's mock them still, as well known as disguised:
Let us complain to them what fools were here,
Disguised like Muscovites, in shapeless gear;
And wonder what they were and to what end
Their shallow shows and prologue vilely penn'd
And their rough carriage so ridiculous,
Should be presented at our tent to us.

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.l:
Ladies, withdraw: the gallants are at
hand.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l:
Whip to our tents, as roes run o'er land.
Exeunt Princess, Rosaline, Katharine, and
Maria.
Re-enter the King, BIRON, LONGAVILLE, and
DUMAIN, in their proper habits.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l:
Fair sir, God save you! Where's the
princess?

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.l:
Gone to her tent. Please it your
majesty
Command me any service to her thither?

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l:
That she vouchsafe me audience for
one word.

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.l:
I will; and so will she, I know, my
lord. Exit.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l:
This fellow pecks up wit as pigeons
pease,
And utters it again when God doth please:
He is wit's pedler, and retails his wares
At wakes and wassails, meetings, markets, fairs;
And we that sell by gross, the Lord doth know,
Have not the grace to grace it with such show.
This gallant pins the wenches on his sleeve;
Had he been Adam, he had tempted Eve;
A' can carve too, and lisp: why, this is he
That kiss'd his hand away in courtesy;
This is the ape of form, monsieur the nice,
That, when he plays at tables, chides the dice
In honourable terms: nay, he can sing
A mean most meanly; and in ushering
Mend him who can: the ladies call him sweet;
The stairs, as he treads on them, kiss his feet:
This is the flower that smiles on every one,
To show his teeth as white as whale's bone;
And consciences, that will not die in debt,
Pay him the due of honey-tongued Boyet.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l:
A blister on his sweet tongue, with my
heart,
That put Armado's page out of his part!

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l:
See where it comes! Behaviour, what
wert thou

Till this madman show'd thee? and what art thou
now?
Re-enter the Princess, ushered by BOYET;
ROSALINE, MARIA, and KATHARINE.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l:
All hail, sweet madam, and fair time of
day!

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l: 'Fair' in 'all hail' is foul, as I conceive.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Construe my speeches better, if you may.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l:
Then wish me better; I will give you
leave.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: We came to visit you, and purpose now
To lead you to our court; vouchsafe it then.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l:
This field shall hold me; and so hold your
vow:
Nor God, nor I, delights in perjured men.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l:
Rebuke me not for that which you
provoke:
The virtue of your eye must break my oath.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l:
You nickname virtue: vice you should
have spoke;
For virtue's office never breaks men's troth.
Now by my maiden honour, yet as pure
As the unsullied lily, I protest,
A world of torments though I should endure,
I would not yield to be your house's guest;
So much I hate a breaking cause to be
Of heavenly oaths, vow'd with integrity.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: O, you have lived in desolation here,
Unseen, unvisited, much to our shame.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l: Not so, my lord; it is not so, I swear;
We have had pastimes here and pleasant game:
A mess of Russians left us but of late.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: How, madam! Russians!

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l: Ay, in truth, my lord;
Trim gallants, full of courtship and of state.

sp.speaker: Ros.
sp.l:
Madam, speak true. It is not so, my
lord:
My lady, to the manner of the days,
In courtesy gives undeserving praise.
We four indeed confronted were with four
In Russian habit: here they stay'd an hour,
And talk'd apace; and in that hour, my lord.
They did not bless us with one happy word.
I dare not call them fools; but this I think,

When they are thirsty, fools would fain have
drink.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l:
This jest is dry to me. Fair gentle
sweet,

Your wit makes wise things foolish: when we
greet,
With eyes best seeing, heaven's fiery eye,
By light we lose light: your capacity
Is of that nature that to your huge store
Wise things seem foolish and rich things but poor.

sp.speaker: Ros.
sp.l:
This proves you wise and rich, for in my
eye,--

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l: I am a fool, and full of poverty.

sp.speaker: Ros.
sp.l:
But that you take what doth to you
belong,
It were a fault to snatch words from my tongue.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l: O, I am yours, and all that I possess!

sp.speaker: Ros.
sp.l: All the fool mine?

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l: I cannot give you less.

sp.speaker: Ros.
sp.l:
Which of the vizards was it that you
wore?

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l:
Where? when? what vizard? why
demand you this?

sp.speaker: Ros.
sp.l:
There, then, that vizard; that
superfluous case
That hid the worse and show'd the better face.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l:
We are descried; they'll mock us now
downright.

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.l: Let us confess and turn it to a jest.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l:
Amazed, my lord? why looks your
highness sad?

sp.speaker: Ros.
sp.l:
Help, hold his brows! he'll swoon!
Why look you pale?
Sea-sick, I think, coming from Muscovy.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l:
Thus pour the stars down plagues for
perjury.
Can any face of brass hold longer out?
Here stand I: lady, dart thy skill at me;

Bruise me with scorn, confound me with a
flout;

Thrust thy sharp wit quite through my
ignorance;
Cut me to pieces with thy keen conceit;
And I will wish thee never more to dance,
Nor never more in Russian habit wait.
O, never will I trust to speeches penn'd,
Nor to the motion of a schoolboy's tongue,
Nor never come in vizard to my friend,
Nor woo in rhyme, like a blind harper's song!
Taffeta phrases, silken terms precise,
Three-piled hyperboles, spruce affectation,
Figures pedantical; these summer-flies
Have blown me full of maggot ostentation:
I do forswear them; and I here protest,

By this white glove,--how white the hand,
God knows!--
Henceforth my wooing mind shall be express'd
In russet yeas and honest kersey noes:
And, to begin, wench,--so God help me, la!--
My love to thee is sound, sans crack or flaw.

sp.speaker: Ros.
sp.l: Sans sans, I pray you.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l: Yet I have a trick
Of the old rage: bear with me, I am sick;
I'll leave it by degrees. Soft, let us see:
Write, 'Lord have mercy on us' on those three;
They are infected; in their hearts it lies;

They have the plague, and caught it of your
eyes;
These lords are visited; you are not free,
For the Lord's tokens on you do I see.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l:
No, they are free that gave these tokens
to us.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l:
Our states are forfeit: seek not to
undo us.

sp.speaker: Ros.
sp.l: It is not so; for how can this be true,
That you stand forfeit, being those that sue?

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l:
Peace! for I will not have to do with
you.

sp.speaker: Ros.
sp.l: Nor shall not, if I do as I intend.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l:
Speak for yourselves; my wit is at an
end.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l:
Teach us, sweet madam, for our rude
transgression
Some fair excuse.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l: The fairest is confession.
Were not you here but even now disguised?

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Madam, I was.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l: And were you well advised?

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: I was, fair madam.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l: When you then were here,
What did you whisper in your lady's ear?

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l:
That more than all the world I did
respect her.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l:
When she shall challenge this, you will
reject her.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Upon mine honour, no.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l: Peace, peace! forbear:
Your oath once broke, you force not to forswear.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l:
Despise me, when I break this oath of
mine.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l: I will: and therefore keep it. Rosaline,
What did the Russian whisper in your ear?

sp.speaker: Ros.
sp.l:
Madam, he swore that he did hold me
dear
As precious eyesight, and did value me
Above this world; adding thereto moreover
That he would wed me, or else die my lover.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l:
God give thee joy of him! the noble
lord
Most honorably doth unhold his word.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l:
What mean you, madam? by my life,
my troth,
I never swore this lady such an oath.

sp.speaker: Ros.
sp.l:
By heaven, you did; and to confirm it
plain,
You gave me this: but take it, sir, again.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l:
My faith and this the princess I did
give:
I knew her by this jewel on her sleeve.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l: Pardon me, sir, this jewel did she wear;
And Lord Biron, I thank him, is my dear.
What, will you have me, or your pearl again?

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l: Neither of either; I remit both twain.
I see the trick on't: here was a consent
Knowing aforehand of our merriment,
To dash it like a Christmas comedy:

Some carry-tale, some please-man, some slight
zany,

Some mumble-news, some trencher-knight, some
Dick,
That smiles his cheek in years and knows the trick
To make my lady laugh when she's disposed,
Told our intents before; which once disclosed,
The ladies did change favours: and then we,
Following the signs, woo'd but the sign of she.
Now, to our perjury to add more terror,
We are again forsworn, in will and error.
Much upon this it is: and might not you To Boyet.
Forestall our sport, to make us thus untrue?
Do not you know my lady's foot by the squier,
And laugh upon the apple of her eye?
And stand between her back, sir, and the fire,
Holding a trencher, jesting merrily?
You put our page out: go, you are allow'd;
Die when you will, a smock shall be your shroud.
You leer upon me, do you? there's an eye
Wounds like a leaden sword.

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.l: Full merrily
Hath this brave manage, this career, been run.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l:
Lo, he is tilting straight! Peace! I
have done.
Enter COSTARD.
Welcome, pure wit! thou partest a fair fray.

sp.speaker: Cost.
sp.l: O Lord, sir, they would know Whether the three Worthies shall come in or no.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l: What, are there but three?

sp.speaker: Cost.
sp.l: No, sir; but it is vara fine,
For every one pursents three.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l: And three times thrice is nine.

sp.speaker: Cost.
sp.l:
Not so, sir; under correction, sir; I hope
it is not so.
You cannot beg us, sir, I can assure you, sir;

we
know what we know:
I hope, sir, three times thrice, sir,--

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l: Is not nine.

sp.speaker: Cost.
sp.p: Under correction, sir, we know whereuntil it doth amount.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.p: By Jove, I always took three times for nine.

sp.speaker: Cost.
sp.p: O Lord, sir, it were pity you should get your living by reckoning, sir.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l: How much is it?

sp.speaker: Cost.
sp.p: O Lord, sir, the parties themselves, the actors, sir, will show whereuntil it doth amount: for mine own part, I am, as they say, but to parfect one man in one poor man, Pompion the Great, sir.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l: Art thou one of the Worthies?

sp.speaker: Cost.
sp.p: It pleased them to think me worthy of Pompion the Great: for mine own part, I know not the degree of the Worthy, but I am to stand for him.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l: Go bid them prepare.

sp.speaker: Cost.
sp.p:
We will turn it finely off, sir; we will
take some care. Exit.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l:
Biron, they will shame us: let them
not approach.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l:
We are shame-proof, my lord: and
'tis some policy

To have one show worse than the king's and his
company.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: I say they shall not come.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l:
Nay, my good lord, let me o'errule
you now:
That sport best pleases that doth least know how:
Where zeal strives to content, and the contents
Dies in the zeal of that which it presents:
Their form confounded makes most form in mirth,
When great things laboring perish in their birth.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l:
A right description of our sport, my
lord.
Enter ARMADO.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.p:
Anointed, I implore so much expense of thy royal sweet breath as will utter a brace of words.
Converse apart wiih the King, and
delivers him a paper.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.p: Doth this man serve God?

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.p: Why ask you?

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.p: He speaks not like a man of God's making.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.p: That is all one, my fair, sweet, honey monarch; for, I protest, the schoolmaster is exceeding fantastical; too too vain, too too vain: but we will put it, as they say, to fortuna de la guerra. I wish you the peace of mind, most royal couplement! Exit.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: Here is like to be a good presence of Worthies. He presents Hector of Troy; the swain, Pompey the Great; the parish curate, Alexander; Armado's page, Hercules; the pedant, Judas Maccabaeus:
sp.l:
And if these four Worthies in their first show
thrive,

These four will change habits, and present the
other five.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l: There is five in the first show.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: You are deceived; 'tis not so.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.p: The pedant, the braggart, the hedgepriest, the fool and the boy:--
sp.l:
Abate throw at novum, and the whole world
again

Cannot pick out five such, take each one in
his vein.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l:
The ship is under sail, and here she
comes amain.
Enter COSTARD, for Pompey.

sp.speaker: Cost.
sp.l: I Pompey am,--

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.l: You lie, you are not he.

sp.speaker: Cost.
sp.l: I Pompey am,--

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.l: With libbard's head on knee.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l:
Well said, old mocker: I must needs
be friends with thee.

sp.speaker: Cost.
sp.l:
I Pompey am, Pompey surnamed the
Big,--

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.l: The Great.

sp.speaker: Cost.
sp.l: It is, 'Great,' sir:--
Pompey surnamed the Great;

That oft in field, with targe and shield, did
make my foe to sweat:

And travelling along this coast, I here am
come by chance,

And lay my arms before the legs of this sweet
lass of France.

If your ladyship would say, 'Thanks, Pompey,'
I had done.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l: Great thanks, great Pompey.

sp.speaker: Cost.
sp.p: 'Tis not so much worth; but I hope I was perfect: I made a little fault in 'Great.'

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l:
My hat to a halfpenny, Pompey proves the best Worthy.
Enter SIR NATHANIEL, for Alexander.

sp.speaker: Nath.
sp.l:
When in the world I lived, I was the
world's commander;

By east, west, north, and south, I spread my
conquering might:
My scutcheon plain declares that I am Alisander,--

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.l:
Your nose says, no, you are not; for it
stands too right.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l:
Your nose smells 'no' in this, most
tender-smelling knight.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l:
The conqueror is dismay'd. Proceed.
good Alexander.

sp.speaker: Nath.
sp.l:
When in the world I lived, I was the
world's commander,--

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.l:
Most true, 'tis right; you were so,
Alisander.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l: Pompey the Great,--

sp.speaker: Cost.
sp.l: Your servant, and Costard.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l: Take away the conqueror, take away Alisander.

sp.speaker: Cost.
sp.p: O, sir, you have overthrown Alisander the conqueror! You will be scraped out of the painted cloth for this: your lion, that holds his poll-axe sitting on a close-stool, will be given to Ajax: he will be the ninth Worthy. A conqueror, and afeard to speak! run away for shame, Alisander. Nath. retires. There, an't shallplease you; a foolish mild man; an honest man, look you, and soon dashed. He is a marvellous good neighbor, faith, and a very good bowler: but, for Alisander,--alas, you see how 'tis,--a little o'erparted. But there are Worthies a-coming will speak their mind in some other sort.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l:
Stand aside, good Pompey.
Enter HOLOFERNES, for Judas; and MOTH,
for Hercules.

sp.speaker: Hol.
sp.l: Great Hercules is presented by this imp,

Whose club kill'd Cerberus, that three-headed
canis;
And when he was a babe, a child, a shrimp,
Thus did he strangle serpents in his manus.
Quoniam he seemeth in minority,
Ergo I come with this apology.

Keep some state in thy exit, and vanish.
Moth retires. Judas I am,--

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.l: A Judas!

sp.speaker: Hol.
sp.l: Not Iscariot, sir.
Judas I am, ycliped Maccabaeus.

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.l: Judas Maccabaeus clipt is plain Judas.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l:
A kissing traitor. How art thou proved
Judas?

sp.speaker: Hol.
sp.l: Judas I am,--

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.l: The more shame for you, Judas.

sp.speaker: Hol.
sp.l: What mean you, sir?

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.l: To make Judas hang himself.

sp.speaker: Hol.
sp.l: Begin, sir; you are my elder.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l:
Well followed: Judas was hanged on
an elder.

sp.speaker: Hol.
sp.l: I will not be put out of countenance.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l: Because thou hast no face.

sp.speaker: Hol.
sp.l: What is this?

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.l: A cittern-head.

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.l: The head of a bodkin.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l: A Death's face in a ring.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l:
The face of an old Roman coin, scarce
seen.

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.l: The pommel of Caesar's falchion.

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.l: The carved-bone face on a flask.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l: Saint George's half-cheek in a brooch.

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.l: Ay, and in a brooch of lead.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l:
Ay, and worn in the cap of a
tooth-drawer.

And now forward; for we have put thee in
countenance.

sp.speaker: Hol.
sp.l: You have put me out of countenance.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l: False; we have given thee faces.

sp.speaker: Hol.
sp.l: But you have out-faced them all.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l: An thou wert a lion, we would do so.

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.l: Therefore, as he is an ass, let him go.

And so adieu, sweet Jude! nay, why dost thou
stay?

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.l: For the latter end of his name.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l:
For the ass to the Jude; give it
him:--Jud-as, away!

sp.speaker: Hol.
sp.l:
This is not generous, not gentle, not
humble.

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.p:
A light for Monsieur Judas! it grows
dark, he may stumble. Hol. retires.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l:
Alas, poor Maccabaeus, how hath he
been baited!
Enter ARMADO, for Hector.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.p: Hide thy head, Achilles: here comes Hector in arms.

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.p: Though my mocks come home by me, I will now be merry.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Hector was but a Troyan in respect of this.

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.p: But is this Hector?

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: I think Hector was not so clean-timbered.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: His leg is too big for Hector's.

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.l: More calf, certain.

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.l: No; he is best indued in the small.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l: This cannot be Hector.

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.p: He's a god or a painter; for he makes faces.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.l: The armipotent Mars, of lances the
almighty,
Gave Hector a gift,--

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.l: A gilt nutmeg.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l: A lemon.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: Stuck with cloves.

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.l: No, cloven.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.l: Peace!--
The armipotent Mars, of lances the almighty,
Gave Hector a gift, the heir of Ilion;

A man so breathed, that certain he would fight;
yea
From morn till night, out of his pavilion,
I am that flower,--

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.l: That mint.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: That columbine.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.l: Sweet Lord Longaville, rein thy tongue.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.p: I must rather give it the rein, for it runs against Hector.

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.p: Ay, and Hector's a greyhound.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.p: The sweet war-man is dead and rotten; sweet chucks, beat not the bones of the buried: when he breathed, he was a man. But I will forward with my device. To the Princess Sweet royalty, bestow on me the sense of hearing.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l:
Speak, brave Hector: we are much
delighted.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.l: I do adore thy sweet grace's slipper.

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.l: Loves her by the foot.

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.l: He may not by the yard.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.l: This Hector far surmounted Hannibal,--

sp.speaker: Cost.
sp.p: The party is gone, fellow Hector, she is gone; she is two months on her way.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.l: What meanest thou?

sp.speaker: Cost.
sp.p: Faith, unless you play the honest Troyan, the poor wench is cast away: she's quick; the child brags in her belly already:
sp.l: 'tis yours.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.p: Dost thou infamonize me among potentates? thou shalt die.

sp.speaker: Cost.
sp.p: Then shall Hector be whipped for Jaquenetta that is quick by him and hanged for Pompey that is dead by him.

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.l: Most rare Pompey!

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.l: Renowned Pompey!

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.p: Greater than great, great, great, great Pompey! Pompey the Huge!

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.p: Hector trembles.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.p: Pompey is moved. More Ates,more Ates! stir them on! stir them on!

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.p: Hector will challenge him.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.p: Ay, if a' have no more man's blood in 's belly than will sup a flea.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.l: By the north pole, I do challenge thee.

sp.speaker: Cost.
sp.p: I will not fight with a pole, like a northern man: I'll slash; I'll do it by the sword. I bepray you, let me borrow my arms again.

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.p: Room for the incensed Worthies!

sp.speaker: Cost.
sp.p: I'll do it in my shirt.

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.p: Most resolute Pompey!

sp.speaker: Moth.
sp.p: Master, let me take you a buttonhole lower. Do you not see Pompey is uncasing for the combat? What mean you? You will lose your reputation.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.p: Gentlemen and soldiers, pardon me; I will not combat in my shirt.

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.p: You may not deny it: Pompey hath made the challenge.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.p: Sweet bloods, I both may and will.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.p: What reason have you for't?

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.p: The naked truth of it is, I have no shirt; I go woolward for penance.

sp.speaker: Boyet.
sp.p:
True, and it was enjoined him in Rome for want of linen: since when, I'll be sworn, he wore none but a dishclout of Jaquenetta's, and that a' wears next his heart for a favur.
Enter MERCADE.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.p: God save you, madam!

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.p: Welcome, Mercade; But that thou interrupt'st our merriment.

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: I am sorry, madam; for the news I bring
Is heavy in my tongue. The king your father--

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l: Dead, for my life!

sp.speaker: Mer.
sp.l: Even so; my tale is told.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l: Worthies, away! the scene begins to cloud.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.p: For mine own part, I breathe free breath. I have seen the day of wrong through the little hole of discretion, and I will right myself like a soldier. Exeunt Worthies.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.p: How fares your majesty?

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.p: Boyet, prepare; I will away tonight.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Madam, not so; I do beseech you, stay.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l:
Prepare, I say. I thank you, gracious
lords,
For all your fair endeavours; and entreat,
Out of a new-sad soul, that you vouchsafe
In your rich wisdom to excuse or hide
The liberal opposition of our spirits,
If over-boldly we have borne ourselves
In the converse of breath: your gentleness
Was guilty of it. Farewell, worthy lord!
A heavy heart bears not a nimble tongue:
Excuse me so, coming too short of thanks
For my great suit so easily obtain'd.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l:
The extreme parts of time extremely
forms
All causes to the purpose of his speed,
And often at his very loose decides
That which long process could not arbitrate:
And though the mourning brow of progeny
Forbid the smiling courtesy of love
The holy suit which fain it would convince,
Yet, since love's argument was first on foot,
Let not the cloud of sorrow justle it
From what it purposed; since, to wail friends lost
Is not by much so wholesome-profitable
As to rejoice at friends but newly found.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l:
I understand you not: my griefs are
double.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l:
Honest plain words best pierce the
ear of grief;
And by these badges understand the king.
For your fair sakes have we neglected time,

Play'd foul play with our oaths: your beauty,
ladies,
Hath much deform'd us, fashioning our humors
Even to the opposed end of our intents:
And what in us hath seem'd ridiculous,--
As love is full of unbefitting strains,
All wanton as a child, skipping and vain,
Form'd by the eye and therefore, like the eye,
Full of strange shapes, of habits and of forms,
Varying in subjects as the eye doth roll
To every varied object in his glance:
Which parti-coated presence of loose love
Put on by us, if, in your heavenly eyes,
Have misbecomed our oaths and gravities,
Those heavenly eyes, that look into these faults,
Suggested us to make. Therefore, ladies,
Our love being yours, the error that love makes
Is likewise yours: we to ourselves prove false,
By being once false for ever to be true
To those that make us both,--fair ladies, you:
And even that falsehood, in itself a sin,
Thus purifies itself and turns to grace.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l:
We have received your letters full of
love;
Your favors, the ambassadors of love;
And, in our maiden council, rated them
At courtship, pleasant jest and courtesy,
As bombast and as lining to the time:
But more devout than this in our respects
Have we not been; and therefore met your loves
In their own fashion, like a merriment.

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.l:
Our letters, madam, show'd much
more than jest.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: So did our looks.

sp.speaker: Ros.
sp.l: We did not quote them so.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Now, at the latest minute of the hour,
Grant us your loves.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l: A time, methinks, too short
To make a world-without-end bargain in.
No, no, my lord, your grace is perjured much,
Full of dear guiltiness; and therefore this:
If for my love, as there is no such cause,
You will do aught, this shall you do for me:
Your oath I will not trust; but go with speed
To some forlorn and naked hermitage,
Remote from all the pleasures of the world;
There stay until the twelve celestial signs
Have brought about the annual reckoning.
If this austere insociable life
Change not your offer made in heat of blood;
If frosts and fasts, hard lodging and thin weeds
Nip not the gaudy blossoms of your love,
But that it bear this trial and last love;
Then, at the expiration of the year,

Come challenge me, challenge me by these
deserts,
And, by this virgin palm now kissing thine,
I will be thine; and till that instant shut
My woeful self up in a mourning house,
Raining the tears of lamentation
For the remembrance of my father's death.
If this thou do deny, let our hands part,
Neither intitled in the other's heart.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: If this, or more than this, I would deny,
To flatter up these powers of mine with rest.
The sudden hand of death close up mine eye!
Hence ever then my heart is in thy breast.

sp.speaker: [Biron.
sp.l:
And what to me, my love? and what
to me?

sp.speaker: Ros.
sp.l:
You must be purged too, your sins are
rack'd,
You are attaint with faults and perjury:
Therefore if you my favour mean to get,
A twelvemonth shall you spend, and never rest,
But seek the weary beds of people sick.]

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.l:
But what to me, my love? but what to
me?
A wife?

sp.speaker: Kath.
sp.l: A beard, fair health, and honesty;
With three-fold love I wish you all these three.

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.l: O, shall I say, I thank you, gentle wife?

sp.speaker: Kath.
sp.l:
Not so, my lord; a twelvemonth and
a day

I'll mark no words that smooth-faced wooers
say:
Come when the king doth to my lady come;
Then, if I have much love, I'll give you some.

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.l:
I'll serve thee true and faithfully till
then.

sp.speaker: Kath.
sp.l: Yet swear not, lest ye be forsworn again.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l: What says Maria?

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: At the twelvemonth's end
I'll change my black gown for a faithful friend.

sp.speaker: Long.
sp.l:
I'll stay with patience; but the time is
long.

sp.speaker: Mar.
sp.l: The liker you; few taller are so young.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l: Studies my lady? mistress, look on me;
Behold the window of my heart, mine eye,
What humble suit attends thy answer there:
Impose some service on me for thy love.

sp.speaker: Ros.
sp.l: Oft have I heard of you, my Lord Biron,
Before I saw you; and the world's large tongue
Proclaims you for a man replete with mocks,
Full of comparisons and wounding flouts,
Which you on all estates will execute
That lie within the mercy of your wit.
To weed this wormwood from your fruitful brain,
And therewithal to win me, if you please,
Without the which I am not to be won,
You shall this twelvemonth term from day to day
Visit the speechless sick and still converse
With groaning wretches; and your task shall be,
With all the fierce endeavour of your wit
To enforce the pained impotent to smile.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l:
To move wild laughter in the throat of
death?
It cannot be; it is impossible:
Mirth cannot move a soul in agony.

sp.speaker: Ros.
sp.l:
Why, that's the way to choke a gibing
spirit,
Whose influence is begot of that loose grace
Which shallow laughing hearers give to fools:
A jest's prosperity lies in the ear
Of him that hears it, never in the tongue
Of him that makes it: then, if sickly ears,

Deaf'd with the clamors of their own dear
groans,
Will hear your idle scorns, continue then,
And I will have you and that fault withal;
But if they will not, throw away that spirit,
And I shall find you empty of that fault,
Right joyful of your reformation.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l:
A twelvemonth! well; befall what will
befall,
I'll jest a twelvemonth in an hospital.

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l:
Ay, sweet my lord; and
so I take my leave.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l:
No, madam; we will bring you on
your way.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l:
Our wooing doth not end like an old
play;
Jack hath not Jill: these ladies' courtesy
Might well have made our sport a comedy.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l:
Come, sir, it wants a twelvemonth and
a day,
And then 'twill end.

sp.speaker: Biron.
sp.l:
That's too long for a play.
Re-enter ARMADO.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.l: Sweet majesty, vouchsafe me,--

sp.speaker: Prin.
sp.l: Was not that Hector?

sp.speaker: Dum.
sp.l: The worthy knight of Troy.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.p: I will kiss thy royal finger, and take leave. I am a votary; I have vowed to Jaquenetta to hold the plough for her sweet love three years. But, most esteemed greatness, will you hear the dialogue that the two learned men have compiled in praise of the owl and the cuckoo? it should have followed in the end of our show.

sp.speaker: King.
sp.l: Call them forth quickly; we will do so.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.p:
Holla! approach.
Re-enter HOLOFERNES, NATHANIEL, MOTH,
COSTARD, and others. This side is Hiems, Winter, this Ver, the Spring; the one maintained by the owl, the other by the cuckoo. Ver, begin.
sp.l: THE SONG.
SPRING.
When daisies pied and violets blue
And lady-smocks all silver-white
And cuckoo-buds of yellow hue
Do paint the meadows with delight,
The cuckoo then, on every tree,
Mocks married men; for thus sings he,
Cuckoo;
Cuckoo, cuckoo: O word of fear,
Unpleasing to a married ear!
When shepherds pipe on oaten straws
And merry larks are ploughmen's clocks,
When turtles tread, and rooks, and daws,
And maidens bleach their summer smocks,
The cuckoo then, on every tree,
Mocks married men; for thus sings he,
Cuckoo;
Cuckoo, cuckoo: O word of fear,
Unpleasing to a married ear!
WINTER.
When icicles hang by the wall
And Dick the shepherd blows his nail
And Tom bears logs into the hall
And milk comes frozen home in pail,
When blood is nipp'd and ways be foul,
Then nightly sings the staring owl,
Tu-whit;
Tu-who, a merry note,
While greasy Joan doth keel the pot.
When all aloud the wind doth blow
And coughing drowns the parson's saw
And birds sit brooding in the snow
And Marian's nose looks red and raw,
When roasted crabs hiss in the bowl,
Then nightly sings the staring owl,
Tu-whit;
Tu-who, a merry note,
While greasy Joan doth keel the pot.

sp.speaker: Arm.
sp.p: The words of Mercury are harsh after the songs of Apollo. You that way; we this way. Exeunt.
